SpaceX will make history with the world's first full recovery of an orbital rocket on Starship Flight 15. Here's when to watch.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note for Nov. 13: Watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch at 5:47 p.m. EST (2247 GMT) in the window above here.

SpaceX is counting down to what might be its most ambitious test flight yet of the company's massive Starship megarocket, the largest launch vehicle ever built.

Today (Nov. 13), SpaceX will launch its next Starship test flight on a mission that, if successful, will return both its Super Heavy first-stage booster and Ship upper stage to Earth for back-to-back landings at their launch pad. It will be the first full recovery of an orbital rocket in history. And if you want to watch it live, you'll need to know what time and where to tune in.

In our guide below, we'll explain exactly when and how to watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission. It is the 15th test flight of the giant stainless-steel reusable rocket, which SpaceX wants to use for everything from Starlink internet satellite launches to landing NASA Artemis astronauts on the moon in 2028, and even for a crewed flight to Mars. But first, SpaceX has to successfully recover and refly both stages, something it's never done before — and that's where Flight 15 comes in. It's the first time the company will try to land an entire Starship rocket. Here's when to tune in.

The Starship Flight 15 test mission is currently scheduled to launch no earlier than Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. But there is a chance of a later liftoff time.

SpaceX has said it has a 75-minute window in which to launch Starship Flight 15 to add some flexibility into its preflight countdown. That means the launch could take place anytime between 5:45 p.m. and 7 p.m. EST (2245-0000 Nov. 14). The local time for the launch window will be 4:45 p.m. to 6 p.m. CST.

SpaceX has not formally announced if it has backup days for the launch, but if the company does have those options, liftoff would likely occur at the same time, based on past Starship missions that saw delays.

One thing that separates Starship Flight 15 from past Starship test flights is its length. The mission, if it runs its full duration, will last just over 22.5 hours until Ship lands back at Starbase. That landing would occur on Saturday, Nov. 14, at 4:17 p.m. EST (2117 GMT). If SpaceX launches at the end of its window on Friday, at 7 p.m. EST, the Ship landing would occur on Saturday at 5:32 p.m. EST (2232 GMT).

Meanwhile, the Super Heavy, known as Booster 22, will land about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

Related: Read our SpaceX Starship and Super Heavy guide for a detailed look at the megarocket.

Starship Die Cast Rocket Model Was $47.99 Now $39.99 on Amazon.

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.

Yes, you'll be able to watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch online, and you have many ways to do so.

Space.com will host a livestream simulcast of Starship Flight 15 on this page, as well as on our homepage and our YouTube channel VideoFromSpace. That webcast will begin about 30 minutes before liftoff, at 5:15 p.m. EST (2215 GMT). However, it may start earlier at 4:58 p.m. EST (2158 GMT), based on a new start time on SpaceX's X account.

SpaceX, of course, will offer its own Starship Flight 15 livestream on its Flight 15 mission page, as well as on its X account. That livestream will also begin 30 minutes before launch, at 5:15 p.m. EST (it's the same one as on Space.com).

If you need your Starship launch preparations fix before the Nov. 13 launch, good news: You can see SpaceX's prep work live online.

NASASpaceflight's YouTube channel offers live views of SpaceX's Starship pads at Starbase 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

On Wednesday (Nov. 11), the channel will stream live views of the Starship Flight 15 rocket stacking, starting at 3 p.m. EDT (1900 GMT).

The NASASpaceflight Flight 15 launch webcast will begin on Nov. 13 at 11:45 a.m. EDT (1645 GMT), about six hours before launch. NASASpaceflight typically offers live commentary and constantly changing views of the Starship launch pad via remote cameras positioned around Starbase.

If there was ever a SpaceX Starship test flight to see in person, this just might be it.

In addition to watching the world's largest rocket launch into space, Starship Flight 15 offers the chance to see both parts of that megarocket return to Earth and be caught in mid-air, 22.5 hours apart.

If you've read our past Starship launch viewing guides, you'll know that SpaceX doesn't have an official viewing site for Starship launches. But you can see the spectacle from several public beaches (as well as private campgrounds). Cameron County Amphitheater at Isla Blanca Park on South Padre Island is always my first recommendation (I watched the first Starship launch from there in April 2023). The park offers a clear view of the Starship launch site across the bay and includes views of boats on the water. There are also bathrooms close by for your convenience. It's 5 miles (8 kilometers) from the launch site as the crow flies. But plan to head out early as traffic can be heavy, especially if you have to cross the bridge from Port Isabel.

Speaking of Port Isabel, there are stretches along Highway 48 between Port Isabel and Brownsville, Texas where you can pull over to the shoulder to watch the launch from 6 to 8 miles (10 to 13 km) away. But it's just the side of a highway, so don't expect bathrooms there. The website SpaceLaunchSchedule.com does report that there are "open pull-offs" to park, from which you can get "wide wetland views." And, of course, it's free. I've driven along Highway 48 during two Starbase visits but have not pulled over to the shoulder to test this site.

If you're on the Mexico side of the border, you may be able to watch Starship Flight 15 from Playa Bagdad, a public beach with a "head-on view of the launch tower and a festive vibe," according to SpaceLaunchSchedule.com.

Finally, there is the Rocket Ranch campground, where you can get a closer view of Starship launches — but you have to pay $200 a ticket (kids under age 17 are $40). The ranch is 3.8 miles (6.1 km) from the Starbase launch site, and your ticket allows you to camp there for one day and one night. Longer four-day stay packages are available.

The Rocket Ranch has two primary viewing locations: The "Outpost" offers the closest view and "unmatched media service," so you can stay connected. The second location is a bit farther away on the campground itself. Please note: Tickets include bus transportation from the ranch campground to a viewing site and back, but it is for one launch attempt only. Be sure to read the full Rocket Ranch FAQ for details on the site.

If everything goes to plan, SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 orbital launch and landing test could last up to 22.5 hours and orbit the Earth 14 times.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in a mission overview.

But the test flight could end early. That's what happened on SpaceX's first orbital Starship test mission, Flight 14 on Sept. 28, which was expected to last nearly 10 hours and orbit Earth six times. Instead, SpaceX ended the mission after three hours and two orbits of Earth as a safety precaution.

"Starship’s initial return to launch site mission is expected to orbit the Earth at an altitude of ~275 km and complete approximately 14 orbits around the planet over the course of a more than 22-hour flight," SpaceX wrote in the mission description. "Similar to Starship’s first orbital mission, the flight profile has been designed with the opportunity to insert into a passively safe suborbital trajectory or safely deorbit at multiple pre-determined areas over the ocean after raising to an orbital altitude."

Super Heavy liquid methane loading begins

Raptor engine chilldown begins on Ship and Super Heavy

Liftoff ("Excitement Guaranteed," SpaceX says)

Hot-staging separation/Ship Raptor engine ignition

Super Heavy boostback burn engine shutdown

Super Heavy landing burn shutdown (followed by 'chopsticks" catch)

Starship orbital insertion engine burn begins

If SpaceX has to end the Starship Flight 15 test flight early, it has three primary splashdown zones to land the Ship upper stage in the ocean.

The company could drop the Ship vehicle in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Hawaii in early and late stages of the mission, according to a reentry overview. A mid-mission splashdown window off the coast of Chile is available if needed at that time. A late-mission splashdown zone in the Gulf of Mexico is also available.

The Gulf is also a wave-off splashdown zone for SpaceX's Starship Super Heavy Booster 22 in case it is unable to land shortly after liftoff.

As with Starship Flight 14, SpaceX is loading Flight 15 with 26 operational Starlink V3 internet satellites. They will be deployed in orbit within the first 90 minutes of the flight.

"The Starship upper stage’s primary objectives include the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites and the first return to launch site and catch at Starbase," SpaceX wrote in its overview. "Starship will only execute a return to launch site if the flight control team has ensured that the vehicle systems critical for reentry maneuvers and final landing burn and tower approach are healthy."

While SpaceX is hoping to launch Starship Flight 15 on time, there is a chance that a technical issue or bad weather could prevent liftoff on Nov. 13.

SpaceX has not announced any official backup days for the Starship Flight 15 launch, but it is likely that the company has at least one if not two additional opportunities to try again, based on past Starship launches. Any backup launch attempts will depend greatly on the nature of a launch delay.

A good website to watch is the official Starbase page for Boca Chica Beach and Highway 4 closure alerts here. Those beach closures can be a good indicator of SpaceX's available flight windows.

You'll be able to follow SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission on Space.com as it happens. Be sure to come back on launch day for complete Starship Flight 15 coverage.

#951. 'My job combines my passion for gaming and football'

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

We're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

So a typical day for us, we'll get a new build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save."

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

So I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a new job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

One of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

Working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

To find out what other jobs you could have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Ever wondered who makes sure your footy video games are great? This guy!

CJ works as an associate quality assurance manager on the video game Football Manager. His team test the game to make sure everything works, and collaborate with the developers to create the most realistic simulation of football.

There are lots of different ways to progress in the gaming industry.

CJ works in the QA (Quality Assurance) team, testing games. In this team, his career progression has followed this path:

His team is just one of the options, though. "There are lots of other roles within the industry too, including production, game design, social media and development, where developers help to code the game," he explains. "Depending on your skills and interests, there are different pathways you can take that you might enjoy and be suited to."

There are different roles in video game testing. CJ notes that: "Salaries can vary depending on your role and the company you work for. They can range from around Â£20,000 to Â£50,000 and upwards." The higher salaries in this range could apply when you've gained more experienced and progressed in your career.

CJ is now a quality assurance manager, but he started out as a quality assurance tester. Find out more about the role of QA tester below. This role can have various other job titles, such as games tester, computer games tester, and video games tester.

You could get into this role via a university course, a college course (such as a Level 3 Diploma in Creative Media, an A-level in Computing, or a T-level in Digital Software Development (England only)), an apprenticeship, or applying directly if you have relevant experience.

#949. Ever wondered what it's like to work on Match of the Day?

Each week the team at the BBC broadcast not one, but two, episodes â bringing viewers all the latest talking points from the Premier League.

Putting on this live broadcast is no easy task, thereâs so many different jobs that get the show to air. BBC Bitesize Careers went behind the scenes on a busy Sunday afternoon to meet just a small number of people involved and to find out more about how they got their jobs on the legendary show.

Cue the music. Do, do, do, dooo, do-do-do-do doooooooâ¦.

Joe Hart on why he loves his job on Match of the Day.

Some took the apprenticeship route whilst others followed their passion for a subject and went on to study it at university. Meanwhile others worked in areas away from sport, and broadcasting, getting different work experience along the way. Make sure to check out the video above to find out more

It goes to show that thereâs no one set way of doing things, and everyone has their own career path to follow. One thingâs for sure though, following your passion can be a great place to start.

Of course you might change your mind or start working in a part of the industry you didnât expect to find yourself in, maybe even change jobs along the way. Itâs all part of making your own career path, and youâll be getting skilled up and banking different experiences along the way.

Bitesize Careers, in partnership with The Open University, has launched the Follow Your Passion campaign, exploring how you can draw on your passions and interests to find your future jobs, with the focus on football.

From content creation to computer game design, nutrition to number-crunching, check out the Bitesize Careers Follow Your Passion collection for loads of inspiring careers content.

#947. Why are some football shin pads so small?

Liverpool striker Lewis Koumas (second from left) sported low socks and small shinpads on his full Premier League debut at Anfield

Liverpool's Lewis Koumas made his full Premier League debut against Manchester City on Sunday.

While doing so, he sported some very low socks over what appeared to be a very small shin pad.

Last season, images of Burnley's Marcus Edwards went viral after the 27-year-old was seen wearing barely visible shin pads during a Premier League match against West Ham.

Two years ago, a picture of teenager Harry Howell celebrating with James Milner while they were Brighton team-mates also gained attention after fans noticed the visible difference in the size of their shin pads.

Howell's 'micro' pair were an obvious contrast to Milner's far more traditional-sized guards.

So what is behind the trend of extra-small shin guards, and why are they used instead of regular-sized pairs?

The simple answer is that players can choose what size shin pads they want to wear.

The International Football Association Board (Ifab), responsible for the laws of the game, say that shin pads are a mandatory piece of equipment players must wear while playing.

Be of an appropriate size to provide reasonable protection and be covered by the socks

And players are responsible for the size and suitability of their shin pads

The law does not define what an "appropriate" shin pad size is, but leave that decision to each individual player.

Shin pads provide vital protection for players to prevent serious injuries.

There has been a rising trend in younger footballers, as well as some big stars, wearing small shin pads during matches.

The reason for this could be for more comfort and to allow players to move around with greater ease.

Referees are only required to check that some form of shin guards are being worn, Ifab told BBC Sport.

Ifab said players - or the parents or guardians of youth players - must take responsibility for their own safety on the pitch.

While shin pad size is ultimately an individuals choice, any decisions around player safety would also be made in consultation with their club and medical staff.

Marcus Edwards last year was seen wearing very small shin pads for Burnley in the Premier League

Grassroots football teams have started to ban small shin pads for safety reasons.

There are concerns that small shin pads do not cover the shins properly, which can lead to an increased risk of injury - especially at non-elite level.

In August 2024, a football club banned small shin pads after a youth player suffered a double leg break.

Penistone Church player Alfie Collins broke his tibia and fibula in a tackle during a game. The teenager's shin pads, which were no bigger than a credit card, were similar to a size recently worn by some stars of the professional game.

Shin pads "play an important role in injury prevention as they are intended to protect the shin from injury", the Football Association said.

"'Micro' or 'mini' shin pads may therefore increase the risk of injury due to the smaller amount of shin covered compared to larger sized shin pads," they added.

#945. Were any current Man City players signed during charges period?

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias has made more than 250 club appearances since his arrival in 2020

No member of Manchester City's current squad was signed during the period in which an independent commission found the club guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations.

Those offences all came between 2009 and 2018. City have denied any wrongdoing and appealed against all of the charges against them.

The club's longest-serving first-team player who was purchased from another club is Portuguese centre-back and club captain Ruben Dias, who joined from Benfica in 2020.

Norway striker Erling Haaland is the next longest-serving arrival, joining from Borussia Dortmund in the summer of 2022.

Midfielder Phil Foden is the only player to have played for the club during the period in which they breached the league's financial rules, but was not a senior signing having come through the club's youth ranks.

Foden, 26, made his first-team debut in a Champions League match against Feyenoord in November 2017.

Like Foden, versatile midfielder Rico Lewis is also a product of the club's academy but did not make his senior debut until August 2022.

All of the club's other senior players were signed between 2023 and 2026.

#944. Who is close to a yellow card suspension in Champions League?

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz is among the players to have received two yellow cards in this season's Champions League

Players will receive a one-match ban should they receive four yellow cards before the semi-finals of the Champions League.

This rule runs from the start of the league phase until the end of the quarter-finals. After then, all yellow cards are wiped out and players cannot be suspended for multiple yellow cards.

Yellow cards that result in a red card during a match do not count towards a player's tally, as a separate suspension will be served.

The same rules apply for both the Europa League and the Conference League.

During the opening three rounds of the Champions League, 16 players received two yellow cards, meaning they are now two cautions away from a one-match ban.

Shakhtar Donetsk's Marlon Gomes, Villarreal's Santiago Mourino and Inter Milan's Hakan Calhanoglu are each on three yellow cards, putting them on the brink of a ban.

Players can also be suspended if they pick up six, eight or 10 yellow cards. This would also result in a one-match suspension every time a player hits an even number of yellow cards above four.

Red cards result in a one-match suspension, with Bayern Munich's Michael Olise missing his side's earlier clash with Arsenal after being sent off against Viking in the previous round of fixtures.

Uefa may increase the length of a red card ban for serious offences such as violent conduct.

*denotes two yellows that resulted in a red card

The following players will miss the next round of league phase matches following either a yellow or red card suspension:

Matheus Cunha (Manchester United - red card suspension)

The Seestar S30 Plus is a great beginner smart telescope for deep-sky imaging, along with a reasonable price tag and enough features to develop your astro skills without buying another instrument.

Excellent deep-sky imaging, even with light pollution

Built-in filters and easy automated set-up

Lower resolution than more expensive smart telescopes

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

I’ve used several smart telescopes over the last few years, but I'd recommend the ZWO Seestar S30 Plus to almost anyone wanting to get started in astrophotography. At $499/€499, it’s a complete imaging system that can photograph galaxies, nebulae and star clusters automatically, even from a light-polluted city. Better still, it’s so small that it can live on a bookshelf.

I recently captured images of the Dumbbell Nebula (M27), the North America Nebula (NGC 7000), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) and the Pleiades (M45) with the S30 Plus. All were remarkably easy to capture, and none of the images accompanying this review required external processing. It’s basically point-and-shoot astrophotography — if you live under light-polluted skies, that’s a game-changer.

I also think the S30 Plus makes an ideal companion to a conventional optical telescope. I can set it to photograph a nebula I have no hope of seeing under light pollution while I try to find brighter objects through the eyepiece of another telescope. It will then get on with collecting photons while I enjoy observing.

For anyone who already owns a telescope but doesn’t want the expense and complexity of conventional astrophotography, that’s a compelling proposition.

One problem with buying a cheap optical telescope is that deep-sky objects rarely resemble the colorful photographs you see online. The moon, planets and bright star clusters can look wonderful through an eyepiece, but faint galaxies and nebulas are much harder to appreciate, particularly from a town or city.

Like all smart telescopes, the S30 Plus gets around that problem by photographing objects rather than showing them directly. Its camera takes repeated exposures, which the telescope automatically stacks to reduce noise and gradually reveal faint detail. The longer you leave it working, the better the resulting image tends to become.

Being able to photograph colorful nebulas without traveling to a remote observing site is one of the biggest attractions of the S30 Plus. For beginners living in cities, it could transform their experience of astronomy.

I’ve always preferred spending my nights looking at the sky rather than fiddling with equipment, which is one reason I enjoy smart telescopes. Traditional astrophotography can involve a camera, tracking mount, adapters, cables, alignment, a laptop and considerable patience before the first useful exposure begins. The S30 Plus removes almost all of that.

I can put it outside, connect the Seestar app and choose a target from its built-in sky atlas. The telescope then moves to the correct position, identifies the star field, centers the object, focuses and begins imaging. Within minutes, a photograph starts appearing on my smartphone. That leaves me free to use an optical telescope alongside it — or stay inside and do something else.

Using the S30 Plus’s built-in UV/IR cut filter — which blocks ultraviolet and infrared light — I captured the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), a popular deep-sky object. As the hours went by, the dust lanes on its outskirts appeared in ever more detail. That’s how smart telescopes work — they collect and combine dozens or hundreds of short exposures, gradually revealing fainter structure while reducing noise.

So impressive is the image after only about five or six exposures that it’s tempting to stop after a few minutes — but patience makes an enormous difference. Fortunately, you don’t have to stand beside the S30 Plus. You can leave it collecting light — even overnight, thanks to its scheduling option (though it’s not waterproof, so check the weather forecast!).

Using the dual-band anti-light pollution filter, the Pleiades open cluster (M45) provided another interesting test. The S30 Plus has a mosaic mode that photographs overlapping sections of sky to create a larger image than its main camera can capture in a single frame. It’s ideal for expansive targets such as the Pleiades and Andromeda, although gathering enough exposures takes time. The app shows how much of the mosaic has been completed, and if needs be, you can continue collecting data on subsequent nights.

I also photographed the Double Cluster in Perseus (NGC 869 and NGC 884) and the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules (M13), both relatively swift targets, but as anyone who’s used a smart telescope knows, it’s the faint nebulas that are the real prize. For those, dark skies mean better data — and that’s exactly why a smart telescope needs to be portable.

The S30 Plus weighs just 3.64 lbs (1.65 kg) and measures 8.25 x 5.5 x 3.15 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm) when switched off. That’s small enough to fit into a camera bag in place of another lens or camera body, which is a major advantage because I travel to remote locations quite frequently. That fact that it sits on such a tiny tripod is also a boon.

I’ve recently used the much larger Seestar S50 Pro, which weighs 6.17 lbs (2.8 kg). It’s a more capable imaging instrument with a 50mm aperture and a larger 8.3-megapixel sensor, but its heavier, bulkier chassis is harder to get into carry-on luggage. The S30 Plus and the higher-spec S30 Pro also differ from the S50 Pro in that they come with a padded carry case. This has a useful carrying handle, although there’s no shoulder strap or dedicated storage for the tripod and magnetic solar filter.

It’s also worth taking along a portable battery and USB-C cable to recharge its built-in 6,000mAh battery during long sessions, though it lasts about six hours, which will suit most observing sessions.

The original, now-discontinued S30 was already impressive, but the S30 Plus is a substantial upgrade. It has improved four-element apochromatic optics with ED glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras, each producing 1,440x2,560-pixel images. That’s almost 80% more pixels than the original S30’s main camera.

The main camera’s field of view has increased slightly to about three degrees, while the wide-angle camera now covers 43.5 degrees of sky. The latter can be used for star trails, though I suspect it’s something most people will experiment with occasionally.

There’s also an EQ mode. This will align the telescope with Earth’s rotation to allow longer exposures and sharper edges, which I found worked really well. It requires an appropriately angled mount or wedge (such as the Seestar TH10 Fluid Tripod Head) and a small tripod.

I tested it at 51 degrees north, which randomly appears to be the cut-off point for ease of use because of the tilt it puts on the telescope. It’s when a tripod begins to topple with the weight, meaning you need a tripod whose legs can be set at a low angle (Seestar’s TC20 tripod would be ideal, and is very compact).

The app makes it all very easy to set up, and advanced imaging possibilities like this are welcome. So, too, is the option of outputting images as lossless FITS files for anyone wanting to process their images using specialist software.

That’s what makes the Seestar S30 Plus such a good beginner’s telescope. It’s easy to use immediately, but there’s plenty of scope to develop more sophisticated astrophotography skills without buying another instrument.

The S30 Plus isn’t limited to deep-sky photography. I photographed a near-full moon against a blue daytime sky, something I particularly enjoy doing with smart telescopes because they’re so quick to set up.

It also comes with a magnetic white-light solar filter, allowing safe photographs of the sun when the filter is securely fitted. This must always be installed before pointing the telescope towards the sun. I did have to manually guide the S30 Plus to the sun and moon on a few occasions, but it’s easy enough to do, and I actually like the option to manually take control — few other smart telescopes allow it. Once you’ve found the sun or moon, the scope centers it and keeps it in view (unless you’re on a moving ship, by the way, where tracking generally fails — something for eclipse chasers to think about).

Planetary photography is less impressive. The 30mm aperture and short focal length aren’t ideal for detailed views of Jupiter or Saturn, so for anyone primarily interested in observing and imaging planets, I’d recommend a conventional optical telescope instead.

The S30 Plus occupies an interesting position in ZWO’s increasingly crowded Seestar range. With dual 8.3MP cameras and wider fields of view, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade from the original S30. Meanwhile, the $999 S50 Pro has a larger 50mm aperture that collects almost three times as much light, although it’s also significantly bulkier and more expensive.

Alternatives exist outside ZWO’s range. DwarfLab’s Dwarf Mini is exceptionally portable, but its lower resolution and more limited capabilities make it less versatile. At the other extreme, Unistellar’s Odyssey has an 85mm aperture, an electronic eyepiece and opportunities to contribute to citizen science projects, but it sits in a different price bracket.

The S30 Plus will hit the sweet spot for many. It offers almost everything a beginner needs to explore deep-sky astrophotography, with built-in filters, mosaic mode and EQ tracking giving plenty of advanced features to grow into. Crucially, it’s small enough to travel with easily. Yes, you can spend more and get slightly better image data, but most beginners don’t need to.

The Seestar S30 Plus is one of the most affordable smart telescopes available, but it’s also one of the best-value offerings in its class.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#942. Which game will Chelsea's Palmer miss after red card?

Cole Palmer was sent off in the second half of Chelsea's 2-0 loss at Stamford Bridge

Chelsea's Cole Palmer will not miss the Blues' Premier League meeting with Manchester United on Saturday, despite being sent off in his side's last Premier League match.

Palmer was shown two yellow cards in the second half of the Blues' defeat by rivals Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. That dismissal meant that Palmer was handed a one-match ban.

The England playmaker was shown his first caution for an off-the-ball incident involving Spurs' Mateus Fernandes. He was then shown a second yellow card for a foul on Conor Gallagher.

In most cases, this would be served in that team's next Premier League match. However, Palmer will not miss Chelsea's meeting with United at Stamford Bridge.

Instead, Palmer will be banned for the Blues' EFL Cup fourth-round match away at Liverpool on Wednesday night.

This is because red card suspensions are carried out across domestic competitions rather than being specific to the competition they were received in.

Suspensions for an accumulation of yellow cards across a campaign are served in the competition in which they are received.

So while the Blues will miss Palmer for their trip to Anfield, he will be available to face United three days after the club's cup tie on Merseyside.

#941. Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row

The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes

They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year.

Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running, but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.

As the Top 100 approaches a decade since its inception, nobody has quite dominated an era like Bonmatí and, while 2025 did not end in major silverware on the European stage, there were moments of sublime brilliance on the way to a Champions League final as well as the Euro one with Spain.

Bonmatí, as the very best do, has become a figure who can step up when needed most, and has become synonymous with the Blaugrana Barcelona stripes, a one-club woman with over 300 appearances in all competitions for the Catalan giants. Catalonia born and bred, both her parents were teachers of the Catalan language, with Bonmatí’s life and career intertwined with the region since she was a child, and now she has become an icon not just at home, but all around the world.

In a time where the women’s game is growing exponentially and world class talents are queueing up to dethrone the midfielder, she remains at the top. However, having broken a leg in training before the Nations League final she will miss more than four months of 2026. She will be sorely missed.

It was a tighter margin of victory in 2025, 453 points ahead of compatriot Mariona Caldentey – compared to 568 last year ahead of Caroline Graham Hansen – with the Spanish duo plus Alessia Russo and Putellas all gaining over 4,000 points from our record panel of 143 judges.

Bonmatí received 43% of the No 1 votes, ahead of Caldentey with a 21% share. Russo and Putellas both had 8% of the first picks in third and fourth respectively.

In a year where England backed up their Euro 2022 success with victory in Switzerland, Brazil continued their dominance in South America and Nigeria regained supremacy in Africa, it was all change across the top 100 as players such as Caldentey, Russo, Hannah Hampton, Temwa Chawinga, Patri Guijarro, Ewa Pajor and Clàudia Pina all made a new-look top 10 for the first time.

The Barcelona starlet Pina was the biggest mover, up 65 places on 2024, followed by another Spaniard in Gotham FC striker Esther González, up 59, while Klara Bühl moved up 40, just ahead of Russo’s 39 to propel the Arsenal striker into the top three.

Ghizlane Chebbak gave Morocco a first ever entry into the top 100 and Canada’s new Northern Super League was represented in its first year thanks to the Nigerian striker Esther Okoronkwo of AFC Toronto.

In fact, almost a quarter of this year’s 100 were brand new faces, emphasising just how fast the women’s game is growing, with the Chelsea and England shot-stopper Hampton the highest of the new names, shooting straight into the top five after her Euro-winning performances, while Vicky López, Sofia Cantore, Nathalie Björn and Michelle Agyemang all made the top 50.

Performances on the continental stage earned first-time appearances for the likes of Okoronkwo, Brazil’s Amanda Gutierres and Nigeria’s Gift Monday, while potential stars of the future such as Olivia Smith, Lily Yohannes and Signe Gaupset ranked for the first time. Mexico’s Charlyn Corral gained long overdue recognition.

Others made their way back into the 100, such as the Arsenal and England duo Leah Williamson and Chloe Kelly after a trophy-laden 12 months while Sandy Baltimore and Cristiana Girelli also made returns straight into the top quarter.

Lucy Bronze, Wendie Renard and Pernille Harder remain the only three players to have maintained a place every year after Saki Kumagai and Jenni Hermoso dropped out for the first time and it was Bronze’s Chelsea who dethroned Barcelona as the team with the most representatives with 15 compared to Arsenal’s 14 and Barcelona’s 12 after a domestic treble for Sonia Bompastor’s side.

Unsurprisingly after another Euro success, England pip Spain as the nation with the most players, 14 to 13, followed by the USA and France with nine each, while Copa América winners Brazil move into the top five for the first time with five players of their own.

The Women’s Super League asserts its dominance with 39 players on the list, up 12 from 2024, ahead of the NWSL with 19 and Liga F with 16. Players such as Jess Park, Aoba Fujino, Mary Fowler and Maya Le Tissier just missed out.

The young and old were once again represented at either end of the spectrum, with Marta again the oldest representative, the 39-year-old playing a key role in Brazil’s Copa América success with a dramatic late goal in the final against Colombia to keep their hopes alive. The OL Lyonnes and USA superstar Yohannes is the youngest at 18 and one of three teenagers to rank alongside López and Agyemang.

But it is again Bonmatí who ranks above them all, asserting her authority as one of the greatest of the modern era.

#940. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Harry Maguire and Alexis Mac Allister are among 13 players on the brink of a one-match ban

The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 13 players sitting on four bookings after 10 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have served a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards)

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four)

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:

Max Dowman - Arsenal (red card suspension)

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension)

Igor Thiago - Brentford (red card suspension)

#936. Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top

The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals

What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature. My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career.

After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure.

Based on those answers, one player stood out above all the others: a kid called Ousmane Dembélé, then a youth player yet to make a first-team appearance at Rennes. Eleven years after appearing in these pages as one to watch, Dembélé has been voted the best male player in the world by the Guardian’s 219-strong voting panel.

Those intangible qualities were in full effect on the night Dembélé made good on his years of promise. The defining image of Paris Saint-Germain’s 5-0 win over Inter in the 2025 Champions League final was not the trophy lift, or any one of the goal celebrations, but Dembélé, poised on the edge of the opposition penalty area, with hunched demeanour and furrowed brow, his face a picture of focus, ready to press. Just how did he get to this point?

One lesson to learn from the Dembélé story: the path to greatness is not always linear. He started off like a train, winning France’s young player of the year award in his first season as a professional. The following season, he helped Borussia Dortmund win the German Cup.

Around that time, in the course of research for my book, Edge, I spoke to Thomas Tuchel, his coach at Dortmund. Tuchel told me that Dembélé’s talent came with an obligation and responsibility to improve. He bracketed his players into one of three “ABC” categories, depending on their dominant motivation, and would change his man-management style accordingly.

The A category stood for “aggressive-motivated”, and referred to players motivated by individual glory and awards (in Tuchel’s eyes, this was not necessarily a negative: think Neymar at Paris).

B stood for “binding-motivated”, those players who love being part of the group and bringing people together (often captains, such as César Azpilicueta at Chelsea).

C stood for “curious-motivated”. These were the players capable of greatness, who needed to be trained in a slightly different way. Their talent could take them far; and on a good day, they were capable of anything. Tuchel loved coaching these players. Dembélé, he felt, was a C.

But the journey was not always smooth. In 2017, he moved to Barcelona, who were flush with money from selling Neymar for €222m (£194m). It was a sliding doors moment. That same summer, Barcelona changed coach: in came Ernesto Valverde; out went Luis Enrique. In six injury-laden years at Barcelona, Dembélé started only a third of the league games. He scored a total of 24 league goals. His most memorable moment might have been missing a last-minute one-on-one in the 2019 Champions League semi-final against Liverpool, when Barcelona were already 3-0 up (remember what happened next? They lost the second leg 4-0). When he did leave, amid mutterings of wasted talent and blackmail, it felt like a relief for all parties.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There is some symmetry to Dembélé’s exceptional 2025. Of the 30 goals he has scored this calendar year at the time of writing, the most decisive and emblematic was probably against Liverpool in the second leg of their Champions League last-16 tie. With PSG 1-0 down from the first leg, Dembélé drifted into his own half, losing his markers who didn’t want to follow him that far. He picked up the ball and spread it wide to the right-winger Bradley Barcola, then sprinted into the box and made it to the cross to score. (He also scored a penalty in PSG’s successful shootout after they won 1-0 at Anfield that night). Dembélé did something similar against Arsenal in the semi-final, dropping deep early in the game, switching the play to the left-sided Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and receiving the return ball, unmarked, on the edge of the area, before scoring. Even when teams knew it was coming, they couldn’t stop him.

At the start of last season, Luis Enrique’s plan was for the whole team to replace the goals of Kylian Mbappé, who had joined Real Madrid. After all, Dembélé had not scored more than 10 league goals in a season since his debut campaign at Rennes. Luis Enrique wanted the team to be the star. And so, with no star player to serve, Dembélé was liberated. This curious-motivated talent who once scored penalties with either foot, and even took corners with either foot, quietly became the main man. He starts the press; his vision, movement, pace, control and positioning set the tone; and his finishing, once considered wasteful, is ruthless.

I still don’t know exactly what makes a good player great but I am closer to an answer. Part of the equation remains what we cannot see: the chemistry within a team, the relationship with a specific coach, playing in a system that brings out the best in every player. But also those other qualities that Dembélé had at 17, and still has now. This well-deserved prize is as much for those attributes as it is for his goals and the trophies he helped Paris Saint-Germain win.

#935. NASA's new UVEX space telescope will peer deep into the universe's most violent events

The UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermaths of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility.

The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum.

UVEX's ultraviolet views will reveal explosive events such as the collisions between ultra-dense stellar corpses called neutron stars and the supernova explosions that mark the deaths of massive stars and the births of neutron stars and black holes. Additionally, the NASA ultraviolet telescope should be able to detect a multitude of low-mass galaxies much closer to the Milky Way than similar galaxies that are currently being observed millions and even billions of light-years away by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

The $590 million UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermath of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions," the mission's principal investigator, Caltech physics professor Fiona Harrison, said in an Oct. 27 statement.

"The first major ultraviolet space mission in two decades, UVEX is a bold leap forward in our exploration of the ultraviolet universe," Caltech President Ray Jayawardhana said in the same statement.

UVEX will benefit from a major leap forward in UV sensitivity thanks to its Caltech-built sensors, which are based on complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) imaging technology. This will help the spacecraft tap into what Harrison described as "the untapped opportunity in the UV."

UVEX will be uniquely poised to spot millions of nearby, small, and faint galaxies that are teeming with infant stars that emit bright UV light.

"In optical light, it's very hard to distinguish these nearby galaxies from faraway ones that look similar," Harrison said. "UV light will make them easier to find."

UVEX won't just be investigating the infancy of stars, however. It will also examine the deaths of ancient stars in the form of supernovas.

Supernovas occur when a massive star runs out of fuel for nuclear fusion and can no longer support itself against the inward push of its own gravity. As the core of the star collapses, its outer layers are blasted outward in cosmic explosions we call supernovas.

This is a process that scientists are keen to understand, as these explosions fling the heavy elements forged during the stars' lifetimes into surrounding galaxies. This material becomes the building blocks of the next generation of stars, planets, and possibly even life.

UVEX will also investigate what happens to the end products of some supernovas, neutron stars, when they meet and merge.

Neutron stars contain between one and two times the mass of the sun crammed into a width of around 12 miles (20 kilometers). That means they are composed of matter so dense that, if a teaspoon of it were brought to Earth, it would weigh over 1 billion tons. That's equivalent to stacking around 9 million adult blue whales on a spoon.

So, when neutron stars in binary systems spiral together and merge, they create an environment so violent that it's the only place in the universe where scientists are sure that elements heavier than lead, like gold, silver, and platinum, are able to be forged.

Currently, neutron star mergers are detected via ripples in spacetime called gravitational waves. Scientists can then follow up on the aftermath of the mergers by observing them in electromagnetic light, from high-energy gamma rays to low-energy radio waves. Thus, UVEX will add another aspect to the investigation of neutron star collisions and our understanding of where heavy elements originate.

The new space telescope's maneuverability will allow it to observe these explosive events very shortly after they happen, giving it an advantage over other instruments, including NASA's long-serving Hubble Space Telescope.

"With UVEX, we will now be able to follow up on gravitational-wave events in ultraviolet light," UVEX team member and Caltech scientist Mansi Kasliwal said in the same statement. "I can count on two hands how many spectra we have of transient events in their infancy phase with the Hubble Space Telescope. Hubble is, of course, amazing and does have some ultraviolet capabilities, but it cannot rapidly pivot to observe real-time events."

UVEX will also be revolutionary in the study of blue stars that have had their outer layers of hydrogen stripped away by companion stars. These stars offer researchers a unique opportunity to study the interior of stars, which is usually obscured by their outer layers.

"We will be able to see what's inside the stars," Kareem El-Badry, an associate professor of astronomy at Caltech and a member of the UVEX team, said in the same statement. "We only know of a small number of stripped stars of this type now. UVEX will find hundreds."

All of the above elements discussed are the expected discoveries and investigations that UVEX will be involved with. Perhaps even more exciting, however, are the unexpected elements of the universe it will uncover.

"Every time you look at the skies in a new wavelength, you learn something new and unexpected," El-Badry said.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

#933. WSL talking points: Tullis-Joyce takes charge and is Shaw the perfect striker?

The City forward hit a WSL hat-trick for the ninth time while Eva Olid’s United have found defensive stability

Not only did Khadija “Bunny” Shaw score a record-extending ninth WSL hat-trick, she scored a “perfect hat-trick” for the fourth time in the competition, something nobody else has managed more than once. Against West Ham the Jamaica striker opened the scoring with her left foot, headed home her second off the underside of the crossbar and tucked in her third with her right foot late on. It helped her side towards a 5-0 win that opened up a two-point gap at the top of the table and stretched Shaw’s lead in the race to be the top division’s top scorer to a five-goal advantage over her nearest challenger, Océane Hurtré. Can anybody stop her relentless pursuit of another Golden Boot? It would appear not. Tom Garry

Are Liverpool getting the points that their performances deserve? Arguably not, on Sunday’s showing. A 2-1 defeat against Arsenal left Gareth Taylor’s side just two places above the automatic relegation zone and just one spot above the relegation playoff place – despite creating plenty of chances and striking the crossbar, as they impressed in possession. Their defender Grace Fisk feels they are on the right path, saying: “Between both boxes I think we’re one of the best in the league, hands down. Sometimes, I’m watching the way our midfield is playing and the way they move, it’s just a joy to watch.” She added: “We gave it a good fight, I hope the fans see that, but it just wasn’t to be.” TG

London City Lionesses kept pace with Manchester City and Chelsea in the race for the WSL title ahead of a huge opportunity to gain ground next week. The Bromley-based side cruised to a 4-1 win against Birmingham on Sunday, keeping them third while moving them four points behind Chelsea, who face the leaders and title rivals City next week. One or both of the two leading sides will drop points at Stamford Bridge, allowing London City to gain ground in the race – if they beat struggling Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium. On the prospect of closing in on their rivals, the Lionesses head coach, Eder Maestre, said: “First we need to have a good result against Arsenal. The Emirates is going to be a very challenging environment so hopefully we can have a very good result and close the gap.” Emillia Hawkins

Manchester United may have a negative goal difference, having scored 10 and conceded 11 in nine WSL games, but they seem to have found the defensive solidity they were missing at the start of the season. Eight of those 11 goals conceded came in their opening three games as Eva Olid’s side adapted to the tactical demands and style of the new manager. “At the start, we didn’t have time together, just three or four weeks, and now we have more time together, I can feel the team improving,” the manager said after the 1-0 win over Aston Villa. “Still a lot of things to keep working on, not everything is perfect, but it’s good to see the way how things are progressing.” The Red Devils have kept three clean sheets in their past five WSL games and against Villa the backline and goalkeeper Phallon Tullis-Joyce were critical. “The opposition had two big chances and Phallon always helps,” said Olid. “I think that we need more confidence. I feel that the confidence is still a little low and it’s something we need to dedicate a lot of time to improve.” Suzanne Wrack

The result may have been crushing for Charlton, who are still yet to pick up a point in the WSL, but there were rare positives for Karen Hills to take from their 3-2 loss to Crystal Palace. It was the first time they had scored twice in a game this campaign and they accrued twice as many shots on target, six to three, than the home side. “At the end of the day, we’re all in this together. We’re all learning,” said Hills after Bethany England’s 90th-minute winner. “We’re all in a new league, playing against new opposition. But we knew Crystal Palace, we know them really, really well, and that game today was us. We played like a Charlton team does and I thought the performance deserved more.” Charlton have proved they can score at this level. Now they need better defensive performances if they are to earn their first points. SW

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

WSL roundup: Crystal Palace deny Charlton first point, London City stay third

Everton put on a display of defensive mettle as they thwarted Chelsea to earn a valuable point at Stamford Bridge. It was a performance that illustrated why they have the joint-second meanest defence in the WSL. The partnership of Naomi Layzell and Rion Ishikawa in the centre of the backline looked resilient once again, making a combined 29 defensive contributions. Layzell herself dominated in the box, making 14 clearances. Full-backs Hannah Blundell and Hikaru Kitagawa were crucial in nullifying the threat posed by Sandy Baltimore and Ellie Carpenter in wide areas. The latter, in particular, has been crucial to Chelsea’s attack this campaign with five goal involvements but was registered just one opportunity on Saturday. The home side, in general, were restricted to chances from set pieces. While creating 20 opportunities on goal, they had an xG of just 0.51 from open play, a clear indicator of how Everton were able to frustrate them. Sophie Downey

Olivia Holdt made her mark for Tottenham Hotspur once again as she put in an eye-catching performance in their 2-1 win over Brighton. With a goal and an assist, the 25-year-old creator proved crucial to Spurs’ ability to complete a second-half comeback. Her impact on their attack was clear to see. Starting on the left, she topped the stats for most touches in the opposition box (10) and most shots taken (4) and proved dangerous whenever in possession of the ball. Her relationship with fellow midfielder Signe Gaupset continues to develop, with Holdt setting up the Norwegian for the equaliser. This was the third consecutive game in which both have scored with Spurs becoming increasingly reliant on the duo as a source of goals. In contrast, Brighton struggled to create. Despite taking an early lead, Arturo Ruiz’s side looked toothless up front, registering just one of their three opportunities on target. SD

#932. Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action

Delap’s talents resurface in style, Gómez delights Brighton with more fireworks, and hair-pulling confusion at Everton

It would have been very easy for Oliver Glasner to lose patience with Liam Delap. The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. Jonathan Wilson

Match report: Nottingham Forest 3-1 Manchester City

Amid the chaotic blur of proceedings at Old Trafford, there was one outstanding performance. Alysson had only one goal to his name in his Premier League career at Aston Villa, but he scored one and helped set up another two in the first 48 minutes against Manchester United. The 20-year-old winger, who has represented Brazil only at under-16 level, was signed from Grêmio for an initial £8.7m last January. His only goal in 18 previous appearances was against Nottingham Forest in September – it took less than a minute to open the scoring at United and less than four for his saved shot to rebound out to Nicolas Jackson for Villa’s second. United’s right-back, Diogo Dalot, was too slow to close Alysson down for his opener and did not have any complaints when his trip on the Brazilian conceded a penalty at the start of the second half. Dalot, often the face of United’s struggles, was booed off when substituted in the second half – Alysson was applauded off by the away end. Billy Munday

Match report: Manchester United 4-4 Aston Villa

Diego Gómez is the latest example of a slow-burning Brighton player given the chance and space to bed in before then flourishing. His current status is as an overnight sensation, though a taste for the spectacular and an eye for goal have been obvious since two goals against Leeds in November 2025. Gómez had signed from Inter Miami that January. The inside-right position from which he drilled his left-foot sidewinder to open the scoring against Brentford brings the best from his shooting prowess with both feet. His October halfway line strike against Crystal Palace came with his right foot. As with a number of Brighton’s purchases, Gómez can play in other positions, variously defensive midfielder, attacking midfielder, even on the wing. Within Fabian Hürzeler’s stringent tactical setup, he is asked to work hard for the ball. Such high pressing created the opportunity Charalampos Kostoulas should have done better with in the moments after the opening goal. John Brewin

There is nothing wrong with Arsenal’s habit of winning games by a single goal: Mikel Arteta’s side did it 15 times on their way to the title last season and the latest against Hull was their fourth this season. Yet despite being six points clear of Manchester City heading into the international break, Arteta will have some concerns about the lack of goals so far. With only 15 from their first 10 matches, Arsenal are on course to break Manchester United’s record of 67 for the fewest by a team being crowned champions in 1993 – the Premier League’s first season. They have also been struggling to score in the first half of games, having gone six matches in all competitions without doing so last month, and Arteta has called on his players to be more ruthless. “Sometimes we try to score the perfect goal against low blocks, but we need to be much more chaotic than that. If we open the scoring much earlier also, it changes the game,” he said. Ed Aarons

All hail Brian Brobbey. It is fascinating that a player sometimes derided for his supposed lack of technical quality while at Ajax has developed into one of the Premier League’s most potent and difficult-to-play centre-forwards in little more than a year in England. His new contract, announced last Wednesday, is richly deserved. There is, as Régis Le Bris acknowledged after the win over Chelsea in which he bullied the visitors, no one quite like him. “Against a team that wants to press like that it’s so important to have a target man,” said the Sunderland manager, and Brobbey was that and then some. Much has been made of how Chelsea miss João Pedro but the Mackems are a different team with their flying Dutchman. Andy Brassell

It was a tale of two benches at Elland Road. The big question hanging over Leeds is whether they have the support for Dominic Calvert-Lewin to make a concerted push for Europe this season; a question that went some way to being answered when the substitutes Harry Wilson and Noah Okafor combined for the latter to score the winner against Tottenham. In contrast, Roberto De Zerbi’s attacking options let him down in a game that felt there for the taking. Dominic Solanke struggled after replacing Mathys Tel, Omar Marmoush looked limited in the central striker role and their brightest performer was the 18-year-old Lucá Williams-Barnett, who, you would suspect, is now not far from a deserved start. Having won three straight games before their defeat in West Yorkshire, Spurs suddenly go into the international break with more questions than answers over their attacking credentials once again. Aaron Bower

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Andoni Iraola had one wish as he signed off for the international window with the 3-1 win at Crystal Palace – that he does not lose any players to injury before Liverpool are back in action against Manchester United at Anfield on Sunday week. The manager is scarred by the previous round of international fixtures: Dominik Szoboszlai, Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak all picked up problems. The trio were missed as Liverpool lost to Manchester City in the first game back. Szoboszlai’s injury was the most concerning: he was only able to return as a substitute in the defeat against Arsenal on 1 November and Iraola said after the win at Palace that the Hungary midfielder was not 100%, that a knee problem required management. “Let’s see if Dom can play with the national team or not,” Iraola said. “I know what I want! But I have to understand the national teams. Also I’m sure Dom will want to go. I’m not sure if it’s going to be fine.” David Hytner

Match report: Crystal Palace 1-3 Liverpool

Bournemouth are really getting to grips with the Thursday-Sunday grind in their first season in Europe. Marco Rose has been working hard to ensure his team are in the right shape to start Premier League games quickly after a Europa League assignment three days earlier. After Thursday’s trip to face Sparta Prague, Bournemouth were quick out of the traps at Ipswich on Sunday, taking the lead through Evanilson after five minutes. “Last week [against Leeds] I said we start slow and this week we start quite quick and score an early goal – I am a magician,” said the head coach, after their eighth consecutive win in all competitions. That equalled a club record set under Eddie Howe in League One. Evanilson is himself on a streak – he’s scored in five in a row in the league – and only Nicolas Jackson has scored as many in the top flight since the last international break. The Brazilian did not need Christian Walton’s helping hand with this goal. BM

Newcastle delivered one of their more convincing performances of the season at Fulham, but one area remains a headache for Matthias Jaissle. Efforts to replace Alexander Isak in attack have not been good enough. Nick Woltemade was loaned to Juventus after an inconsistent debut season in England and there was not much encouragement to take from how Yoane Wissa and William Osula played at Craven Cottage. Wissa, who has struggled since his £55m move from Brentford last summer, has four goals in 41 appearances and did not put himself about enough before being taken off after 61 minutes, while Osula did not manage a touch in Fulham’s area and lost possession before Rodrigo Muniz’s late equaliser for the hosts. Jaissle needs more from his forwards on and off the ball. Otherwise Newcastle are going to need to find different players to lead their attack. Jacob Steinberg

The laws on hair-pulling were changed for this season after the red cards that were issued to Michael Keane, Lisandro Martínez and Dan Ballard in 2025-26. They are undoubtedly an improvement but, as James Tarkowski’s pull on Caleb Yirenkyi’s hair demonstrated in Everton’s comeback against Coventry, grey areas remain. Frank Lampard and David Moyes agreed the Everton captain should not have been sent off as there was no excessive force involved. But was it “a clear action without excessive force” that should have resulted in a yellow card for unsporting behaviour and a penalty to Coventry? Or “negligible, accidental or inadvertent contact” that is not usually considered an offence? Moyes offered up one solution – scrap the law altogether. “I think it is still ridiculous that is even categorised in the rules of the game,” the Everton manager said. “I can’t understand why they don’t fix this completely because I don’t see it as a good rule at all.” Andy Hunter

#930. Novel CRISPR therapy is poised to gain first FDA approval to alter genes inside the body

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

The Cas9 protein together with RNA and DNA (orange; artist’s illustration). A new therapy uses the CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing system to treat a rare genetic disease called hereditary angioedema.Credit: Alfred Pasieka/Science Photo Library

A pioneering therapy that edits genes inside a recipient’s body continues to be effective four years after treatment, according to data released by its developer, Intellia Therapeutics.

The therapy, named lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z), was designed to treat one form of a genetic disorder that causes episodes of painful and potentially dangerous swelling in the throat and other parts of the body. Lonvo-z deploys the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing system to disable the gene that produces prekallikrein, a protein made in the liver that promotes blood-vessel leakage.

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Intellia, headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has applied for approval of lonvo-z to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which is expected to issue a decision by 10 March. If approved, the therapy will become the world’s first CRISPR medicine to be delivered directly inside the body, or in vivo, John Leonard, Intellia’s chief executive, told investors on 12 November. Currently, the only CRISPR therapy approved by the FDA is performed on cells that have first been removed from the body and are subsequently re-infused.

For people with the condition, hereditary angioedema, the gene-editing approach could offer relief from a lifetime of juggling medications to prevent and treat swelling attacks, says Jonathan Bernstein, a hereditary angioedema specialist at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio and an investigator on a lonvo-z trial. “It’s very reassuring,” he says of the four-year data. “That’s what you’re supposed to see.”

The only approved CRISPR therapy is Casgevy, a treatment for two genetic blood disorders, sickle cell anemia and ß-thalassemia. To create a dose of Casgevy, physicians first remove blood stem cells from the recipient, then send them off for gene editing. The edited cells are infused back into the recipient.

The therapy must be made anew for each person, adding time, cost, and complexity. The recipient also has to undergo harsh chemotherapy treatment to make room for the edited cells.

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

In vivo gene-editing approaches aim to sidestep these concerns by editing genes directly in the body. Lonvo-z, for example, consists of fatty particles that encase mRNA encoding CRISPR-Cas9 components. The particles are infused into the blood and taken up by the liver, where prekallikrein is produced. The procedure takes one day.

In vivo gene editing can introduce other safety concerns, however. The therapy affords no opportunity to screen out cells with unwanted edits at other locations in the genome, or in other organs. Recipients might also have harmful immune responses to the treatment.

Last year, the FDA placed a clinical hold on two other in vivo studies sponsored by Intellia after a participant — an older man with other health conditions — developed liver damage and died after receiving a CRISPR treatment. The FDA lifted the hold this year after requiring added safety measures.
