It was a window that revealed the extent of The Friedkin Group’s ambitions, the strength of the club’s finances after the move to a new stadium, the state of the relationship between the manager and chief executive and the expertise of the senior leadership team; and none of it was positive. The owners deserve some credit for listening to fans and halting the self-defeating sale of Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest but otherwise it was a modest window that descended into a shambles. The club’s best player was sold for a below-market fee, a move for Folarin Balogun collapsed and although the equally desperate search for a right-back ended with Ainsley Maitland-Niles signing, David Moyes was left with one striker and a smaller squad than he started the day with, despite repeatedly urging his employers to strengthen. AH

It was a summer of change at Craven Cottage. Marco Silva departed after five successful years in charge and was replaced by the inexperienced Álvaro Arbeloa, who has focused on adding youth. Gonzalo García, César Palacios and Manuel Ángel followed Arbeloa from Real Madrid and Shea Charles is an exciting signing from Southampton. Some stalwarts have left. Raúl Jiménez joined Wolves and Harry Wilson went to Leeds. Fulham looked to strengthen. They secured the midfielder Hugo Larsson and centre-back David Affengruber on deadline day but missed out on another target, the right-back Andrei Ratiu. JS

“Think of us like a volcano,” said Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali, in early July. “It’s boiling right now and it’s going to erupt.” Two months on the Ilicali has presided over 18 signings, investing more than £150m and his manager, Sergej Jakirovic, has choreographed two Premier League wins. The horizon looks infinitely brighter than in June, when the playoff winners sold two players for a combined £8.5m to avoid breaching English Football League spending rules and a near-certain six-point deduction. Hull, remember, spent last season under a two-window EFL transfer embargo. They have compensated for that this summer and, although time will tell whether all those new faces are compatible, reasons for optimism remain real. Not least because last season’s cult hero loanee forward Joe Gelhardt has signed permanently from Leeds. Louise Taylor

Key ins: Nobel Mendy (Rayo Vallecano, £20m), Konstantinos Tzolakis (Olympiakos, £20m), Lucas Herrington (Colorado Rapids, £17.1m), Ilyas Ansah (Union Berlin, £14.5m), Mohamed-Ali Cho (Nice, £13m), Brooke Norton-Cuffy (Genoa, £12m), Jens Hjerto-Dahl (Tromsø, £10m), Tim Iroegbunam (Everton, £13m), Christos Mouzakitis (Olympiakos, £12.9m), Sorba Thomas (Stoke, £7.5m), Joe Gelhardt (Leeds, £6.5m), Jack Butland (Rangers, £3.5m), Lucas Gourna-Douath (Red Bull Salzburg, £3.4m), Elliot Stroud (Mjällby, £3m), Robinio Vaz (Roma, loan), Hidemasa Morita (Sporting, free), Matt Targett (Newcastle, free), Óscar Zambrano (Maribor, undisclosed fee)

Key outs: Ivor Pandur (Rangers, £6m), Cody Drameh (Genoa, £3.9m), Abu Kamara (Portsmouth, £2.5m), Kyle Joseph (Middlesbrough, undisclosed fee)

The late addition of Burnley’s striker Zian Flemming brought Ipswich’s summer spend close to £200m. That appears to be the cost of giving yourselves a genuine shot at survival. Arrivals such as Exequiel Palacios and Julio Enciso should have no business in the lower reaches, and the former Fulham pair Sasa Lukic and Issa Diop add crucial experience. Gary O’Neil can call upon enviable depth in midfield and speed on the flanks, where Abdul Fatawu and Daizen Maeda look sharp. But time will tell whether Ipswich strengthened their defence sufficiently for regular tests of the kind they failed at Old Trafford on Sunday. Nick Ames

Key ins: Julio Enciso (Strasbourg, £26m), Emersonn (Toulouse, £24m), Exequiel Palacios (Bayer Leverkusen, £23.5m), Zian Flemming (Burnley, £20m), Abdul Fatawu (Leicester, £20m), Abdoul Ouattara (Strasbourg, £17m), Florentino Luís (Burnley, £16m), Daizen Maeda (Celtic, £10m), Sasa Lukic (Fulham, £9m), Kjell Scherpen (Union St-Gilloise, £8.6m), Issa Diop (Fulham, £8.5m), Chuba Akpom (Ajax, £7m), Kayne van Oevelen (Volendam, £3.4m), Cédric Kipré (Reims, £1.7m)

In an ideal world Daniel Farke might have wished for one more high-calibre attacking recruit but that should not detract from a very decent window, featuring seven extremely sensible signings. The importance of the acquisition of the England goalkeeper James Trafford from Manchester City should not be underestimated. Trafford will almost certainly provide Leeds with a few more extra points – not to mention enhance their play courtesy of his stellar footwork. Just in front of him Tarik Muharemovic looks an outstanding defensive buy. Harry Wilson raises creativity levels and the attacking tone. LT

Key ins: James Trafford (Manchester City, £40.5m), Tarik Muharemovic (Sassuolo, £34.1m), Nico Elvedi (Borussia Mönchengladbach, £6.8m), Michael Zetterer (Eintracht Frankfurt, £4.3m), Jean-Mattéo Bahoya (Eintracht Frankfurt, loan), Melvin Bard (Nice, loan), Harry Wilson (Fulham, free)

The final window of Richard Hughes’s spell as sporting director raised more questions over Liverpool’s direction under Fenway Sports Group, owners soon to be enriched by a £2bn investment from 1892 Holdings. The shift towards paying big money for big names continued with Bradley Barcola’s arrival from Paris Saint-Germain while Jérémy Jacquet and Victor Muñoz followed the older policy of developing young potential. Yet weaknesses remain at right back, defensive midfield and on the right wing, where Mohamed Salah’s exit was foreseen from December. Squad depth is lacking and a lot rests on the return to full fitness of Hugo Ekitiké, Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni. AH

Key ins: Bradley Barcola (PSG, £123m), Jérémy Jacquet (Rennes, £55m), Víctor Muñoz (Osasuna, £34.5m), Ronald Araújo (Barcelona, loan)

Key outs: Curtis Jones (Inter, £25.7m), Harvey Elliott (Valencia, loan), Mohamed Salah (Trabzonspor, free), Ibrahima Konaté (Real Madrid, free), Andy Robertson (Tottenham, free)

With Enzo Fernández’s deadline day signing for a British record-equalling £125m, Enzo Maresca can have zero complaints about a first window as Manchester City’s head coach. The No 8 follows two No 6s, in Elliot Anderson (£116m) and Ayyoub Bouaddi (£85m), and the wide players Allan Elias (£34m) and Iliman Ndiaye (£60m plus £5m) as major signings, the total spend on incomings about £457.5m. Factor in how City have generated about £281.8m in outgoings for a net spend of £175.7m, the divisions third-biggest of the window, and this sizable investment has to work - particularly the acquisition of Fernández. Jamie Jackson

Bernardo Silva (Real Madrid, free)

This was the window of the midfielder for Manchester United, with three recruited: Youri Tielemans (a No 8), Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba (No 6s). Yet missing was a left-back despite the targeting of Lewis Hall, and others, plus reinforcements for the rest of a creaking rearguard. The reason? A lack of money or, maybe, a reluctance to spend unless the finance was generated by transfers. Manuel Ugarte’s long-term injury (preventing his sale) and Joshua Zirkzee’s reluctance to move were factors. Will the specialist Luke Shaw, plus the stand-in options of Parick Dorgu (a wing-back/left forward), Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui (right-backs), Lizandro Martínez (centre-back) and Baleba prove adequate? JJ

Key outs: Rasmus Højlund (Napoli, £43.2m), Casemiro (Inter Miami, free)

Newcastle describe their transfer window as “transformative” and, with reinvention the name of the game on Tyneside, it is easy to see why. After selling Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães for a grand total not too far off £250m, they have signed eight – mainly young – players. Along the way the spine of a team now managed by Matthias Jaissle rather than Eddie Howe has been renewed and new cult heroes including the former Benfica right-back Amar Dedic and the former Manchester City midfielder Nico González are emerging. The deadline day arrival of the exciting 21-year-old Belgium forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille is regarded as quite a coup. Have Newcastle choreographed a triumph from a window that, at one point, looked potentially disastrous? LT

Receiving £116m for Elliot Anderson was proof that among the chaos in recent years, Forest have carried out some smart recruitment. After appointing Oliver Glasner, the club worked to provide for his needs, splashing out on Ousmane Diomande, while Xaver Schalger was a sensible acquisition for free, as was Daniel Muñoz at £22m. A No 9 was the priority and it required a club record £45m to acquire the long-term target Liam Delap, who fits the bill perfectly. Whether not sourcing a direct replacement for Anderson will hurt them remains to be seen but at least they did not panic, making it a measured window where they were able to trim the squad. Will Unwin

After last summer’s 14 new faces this had been a bit of a conservative, almost slightly underwhelming, window. Or at least it was until Crystal Palace tried to hijack Sunderland’s agreement to sign the Lyon winger Malick Fofana and the two Premier League clubs engaged in an astonishing deadline day tug of war involving private jets from both sitting on the tarmac at Lyon airport and Fofana undergoing a medical in France unsure as to his destination until finally choosing Wearside. Arguably Sunderland’s biggest achievement was keeping last season’s star players. If persuading Granit Xhaka to stay rather than defect to Chelsea was vital, Régis Le Bris will be similarly delighted to have retained widely admired individuals of the calibre of Enzo Le Fée, Robin Roefs and Noah Sadiki. LT

A comprehensive reboot, from back to front, featuring a club record outlay for a window and one of the most lavish by any club ever. In the first summer window since the departure of the longstanding chair Daniel Levy, the hierarchy have backed Roberto De Zerbi in an attempt to put the trauma of last season behind them. All the new signings have Premier League experience and – apart from Mateus Fernandes and Sávio – are aged 25 or over. In other words, they ought to be ready to hit the ground running. The opening two matches did not go to plan. It will get better. Won’t it? David Hytner

#874. SpaceX launches 2nd mystery mission for US Space Force in 6-day span (video, photos)

SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such flight for the company in a six-day span.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627.

Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast.

We don't know much about USSF-627 or USSF-432; both are classified. Some experts have speculated, however, that each mission launched a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military branch track potential targets around the world.

SpaceX didn't reveal details about either USSF-627 or USSF-432, and the company ended the webcast of both launches shortly after the first stages of their Falcon 9 rockets came back to Earth.

In both cases, that touchdown occurred about 8.5 minutes after liftoff on the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange of Vandenberg in the Pacific Ocean.

It was the seventh mission for USSF-627's Falcon 9 booster, which carries the designation 1103.

NROL-179 | SDA-T1TL-E | SDA-T1TL-A | 3 Starlink missions

USSF-627 was the 120th Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the rocket's 15th national-security flight of the year to date. Eighty-five of the 120 flights have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink broadband constellation in low Earth orbit, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.

The Falcon 9 is not on a record-breaking cadence this year. In 2025, the rocket flew a whopping 165 missions, and 122 of them were Starlink flights.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#872. The chaos that took Carrick from two-year deal to sacked within 15 games

Six PL games that defined Carrick's Man Utd tenure

It was just after 6pm on Sunday, 8 November when the message landed. Manchester United were 4-2 down to Aston Villa, and Old Trafford was resigned to defeat.

The plea came from someone who knows Michael Carrick well, has worked with him and understands at first hand the pressures of life in the United goldfish bowl.

As it turned out, the predicted ending did not come to pass.

United scored twice in stoppage time to salvage a 4-4 draw. Carrick celebrated Patrick Dorgu's equaliser by raising an arm in the air. After that, he walked round the pitch on what has turned out to be a final lap of appreciation.

As the United supporters sang his name, Carrick placed himself in the middle of his players to ensure the fans did not turn on them in the way they had done after the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth two weeks before.

It was a decision that summed up the 45-year-old - supporting the collective, rather than looking after himself.

That obvious desire to do the best for his club and his players - and his storied past - explains why Carrick's song continued to be bellowed from the stands when just about everyone else involved at United was attracting fury and derision.

To get this far is longer than many envisaged. It seemed there was no way Carrick could survive the Bournemouth debacle.

United took 44 hours to communicate to the wider world they were sticking with him then, though it is understood Carrick was told the day before.

Since then, it has been chaos. United have won one, drawn one and lost one.

Outstanding in the opening 45 minutes at Chelsea, they conceded at the start of the second half before defender Lisandro Martinez was sent off for two bookings in the space of five minutes. They lost 2-0.

Awful and two goals down inside 17 minutes against Roma in the Champions League, they roared back with the kind of thrilling comeback Carrick was part of so often during Sir Alex Ferguson's days to win 3-2.

Then, Villa. Two goals down in four minutes thanks to calamitous goalkeeping, they clawed back to level before half-time. More abysmal defending left United with another mountain to climb - but they emerged from the carnage with a point.

Try picking the bones out of that. Had Carrick's stock increased, or had it merely proven he was not the right man the job? United decided it was the latter.

United came from two goals down twice to snatch a draw against Villa

Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox celebrated Dorgu's stoppage-time equaliser against Villa in the directors' box. But they had a slightly detached perspective.

Within days they were flying to Monaco to tell minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe change was required.

For the third season in a row, United are replacing the man in charge of the team mid-season.

Unlike with Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim, this decision is not a surprise. Not because of what is happening now, but because what is happening now is so at odds with what happened last season.

After 12 wins in 17 games under Carrick and a return to the Champions League, the mood in pre-season was overwhelmingly positive.

There were no signs of splits, young players including JJ Gabriel were part of the group, and senior staff spoke optimistically about the potential of Bruno Fernandes' proposed partnership with Youri Tielemans.

Recruitment was clearly an issue, but more of that later.

Man Utd fan wants to know why Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada haven't been sacked

Looking back, the 48 hours before United's season-opening match at Hull were pivotal.

With Benjamin Sesko still trying to ease his way back from the shin issue that ended his previous campaign early, Amad Diallo suffered an ankle injury that would rule him out for seven weeks. It meant Carrick was deprived of his first-choice striking alternative, with Bryan Mbeumo having to play on the right of the attack.

Carrick instead turned to Matheus Cunha, whose preference for dropping deep took him into the spaces captain Fernandes likes to occupy.

It neutralised United's attack on a day they seemed ill-prepared to meet the physical challenge of an opponent motivated by their long-awaited Premier League return.

In his role as interviewer for Nordic broadcaster Viaplay, former Norway and Middlesbrough striker Jan Aage Fjortoft claimed United had lacked passion - something Carrick dismissed as "ridiculous".

"It's one game," Carrick told the media afterwards.

The following week, United were losing to Ipswich - another newly promoted side. Only a slip from Marcelino Nunez inside his own half allowed Cunha to tee up Fernandes for an undeserved equaliser. Fernandes, who had just been crowned PFA Player of the Year for 2025-26, went on to complete a hat-trick in a 5-2 win.

United have not won in the Premier League since.

After that came a trip to Everton. Twice United led, the second time when Sesko struck two minutes from time after coming on as a substitute. Deep into stoppage time, Ainsley Maitland-Niles drove home from long range to deny the visitors.

Asked how confident he was in his side's ability to react to a disappointing start to the season, Carrick snapped back: "It's not been that bad."

Manchester United's 4-1 defeat by Como was one of their worst European results

Time and again, United's fitness was called into question. They struggled badly against a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men in the first half before City benefited from an Erling Haaland goal that referees' chief Howard Webb later admitted should not have stood.

Carrick's complaints after the match were justified - but they masked a poor performance from his team.

After taking a 2-0 lead inside 10 minutes against Brighton in the EFL Cup, United were outplayed and beaten, thanks to two goals in four second-half minutes.

Carrick's coaching staff - lauded months earlier - could not find an answer.

The head coach said Cunha's injury-time equaliser against a Fulham side who started the game bottom was a positive to build on. But immediately after the international break, United were held to another draw - conceding in injury time to an out-of-form and 10-man Tottenham.

The familiar downward spiral was getting out of control.

Martinez was at fault for Spurs' leveller, which made his post-match outburst after the 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid more amazing.

The Argentina defender criticised United's summer recruitment and placed the blame at the door of "the technical director" - Wilcox.

By the time of Martinez's outburst, Sesko and left-back Luke Shaw were injured. Marcus Rashford has not played since. The rotation at left-back eventually led to Carrick starting five different players in that role.

After conceding in the opening minute against Atletico, Como scored inside the first two in a 4-1 win. Fernandes came out afterwards and criticised Carrick's tactics.

He was dropped for the Bournemouth game, but returned as captain at Chelsea.

Sesko has started two games and scored two goals this season

There is no doubt Carrick made mistakes. The Hull game - a performance that set the tone for the season so far - was inexplicable.

But it is also fair to wonder how much he was let down by the recruitment side.

A source close to one player questioned why so much attention was focused on midfield, when the inevitable consequence was Fernandes being shifted away from the central position he excelled in over the second half of last season.

Casemiro's exit necessitated a big-money replacement but, after heading down one-way streets in the pursuit of Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest and Mateus Fernandes from West Ham, it was 25 August before the Â£70m deal to sign Carlos Baleba from Brighton was completed.

A pre-existing ankle injury meant Baleba did not make his debut until 10 October. After starting only five games, he is now out for an extended period with a hamstring problem.

Tielemans arrived from Aston Villa for Â£35m and Andrey Santos signed from Chelsea in a deal that could eventually cost Â£50m. The former scored his first goal in the Villa thriller. Santos, though, was left on the bench. He has started four league games.

Meanwhile, obvious issues in Carrick's squad were left unaddressed.

Shaw started every Premier League game last season, but that was an outlier in an otherwise injury-hit career. Clear competition was needed in that area. Instead, United backed off, thinking they might be able to sign Lewis Hall from Newcastle next summer.

United's back four for the first home game of the season was the same as it was for the first home game under Ten Hag in 2022. They have conceded 30 goals so far this term - the most of any team in Europe's top five leagues, apart from Lens.

Up front, Sesko finished last season injured and had only made two substitute appearances when the transfer window closed. Carrick subsequently admitted he would be out for a "long time" - thought to be at least January.

United's players were booed down the tunnel by their own fans after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth

Carrick was asked about the possibility of further signings following the arrivals of Tielemans and Santos during the club's pre-season training camp on 13 August.

"We want more, we need more," was the response.

For someone so calm and considered, it was a strong demand for action to those above. Well-placed sources say it was obvious to Carrick where the holes in his squad were and he was expecting more than a single new signing from that point.

A couple of weeks before Carrick spoke, another club source told BBC Sport that United should be judged when the transfer window closed.

From this position, that judgement would have to be negative.

However, other United sources defend the recruitment strategy, claiming it easy to be wise after the event and at the end of last season, Kobbie Mainoo was their only orthodox midfield option.

It is also argued the United squad is capable of finishing in the Champions League places.

More than a quarter of the way into the season, they are some way off that target.

Carrick has paid the price - lasting less than six months into the two-year contract he signed in May.

Mauricio Pochettino will be his replacement. Berrada and Wilcox will hope his appointment brings calm after another period of chaos.

#871. Record-breaking Ebola outbreak: phone data reconstruct first weeks of spread

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Confirmed infections of Bundibugyo Ebola have surpassed 10,000 in the DRC since May.Credit: Xinhua/Shutterstock

Epidemiologists have used mobile-phone data and test records to map the early spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)1 weeks before the outbreak was declared. The authors say the study findings reveal how surveillance systems failed to detect signals of the disease early on and enabled it to spread rapidly.

It is now six months since the outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of the virus was announced. The number of confirmed infections has risen to more than 10,000 and 5,198 people have died, making this the largest Bundibugyo outbreak so far. There are no licenced vaccines or approved treatments specifically for Bundibugyo, which has complicated efforts to control it.

The DRC declared the outbreak on 15 May after laboratory tests confirmed the first case, a person from Ituri province in the country’s northeast, was infected with the Bundibugyo strain. Around the same time, suspected cases were being reported in several DRC locations, including Mongbwalu, Rwampara, Bunia and Nyankunde in Ituri, and Butembo, Katwa and Goma in the neighbouring province of North Kivu. The World Health Organization declared the outbreak a public health emergency of international concern on 17 May, citing infections among health-care workers, the geographical spread of cases and clusters of undocumented deaths. Researchers strongly suspect that the virus had been spreading in the region months earlier.

To understand how the outbreak spread so quickly, the researchers looked at anonymized mobile-phone data to trace the movement of people between areas.

Although the first confirmed case was identified on 15 May, the study reports that the person had symptoms as early as 25 April.

The team found that people travelling out of Mongbwalu, Bunia and Rwampara between 24 April and 24 May helped to predict which health zones would report infections by 1 June. For instance, areas close to the initial centres were at greater risk of infections, the study found.

The risk of infections rose again in places 150–200 kilometres away from the initial outbreak centres because people travelled to larger towns and cities along established routes, says study co-author Pierre Akilimali, an epidemiologist at the National Institute of Public Health (INSP) in Kinshasa.

The authors say the findings show that people movement was a key driver of the rapid spread in the early phases of the outbreak.

“These are very important findings which reinforce what we initially knew at the onset of the outbreak,” says Tambe Akem, an independent public-health consultant based in Yaoundé, Cameroon.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03666-z

Ebengo. D. M. et al. Science https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aej4586 (2026).

"There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our universe, much less two."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have discovered the oldest pair of supermassive black hole-powered quasars ever seen. There's just one problem: they shouldn't exist!

The compact quasar pair, spotted with the aid of the Gemini North telescope, has been designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, which means "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the universe." The compact quasar pair is seen as it was 900 million years after the Big Bang at a time when such supermassive black holes should not have had time to grow to such tremendous masses.

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua isn't just the oldest and most distant quasar pairing ever seen. There is just 18,100 light-years, or roughly one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way, between the supermassive black holes, which have masses of 1.5 billion and 400 million times that of the sun. That makes Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua the most compact quasar pair found during a period of the universe's history known as Cosmic Dawn, shortly after the birth of the first stars, galaxies, and black holes.

"There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our universe, much less two," research team leader Silvia Onorato of the NOIRLab said in a statement.

"We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the universe was only a thirteenth of its age and, astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today."

Quasars occur when the supermassive black holes that sit at the heart of large galaxies are surrounded by a flattened cloud of swirling gas and dust called an "accretion disk," from which they feed or "accrete" matter. The immense gravity of the central black hole causes friction, heating the accretion disk and causing it to glow, often brighter than the combined light of every star in the surrounding galaxy. We see that glow as a quasar.

Finding such objects in the recent cosmic history of the 13.8-billion-year-old universe isn't troubling, though finding compact pairs of them is still extremely rare. Such pairs should be common because the merger of galaxies that brings together supermassive black holes is frequent. That should lead to an abundance of pairs of quasars with a separation less than the typical size of a galaxy. There are three reasons this has proven tricky. Firstly, the "quasar phase" of a supermassive black hole is relatively short on cosmic terms. Secondly, even relatively close quasar pairs are very far away, making them faint and hard to detect with ground-based telescopes. Finally, at such great distances and with such a small separation between the two supermassive black holes, the individual members of a quasar pair are hard to individually resolve.

Yet, astronomers do find quasar pairs. Sometimes at distances and times that they would probably rather not, because it challenges everything we know about black hole growth.

The trouble arises before the universe was 1 billion years. That is because, according to current models, black holes should need at least 1 billion years to feed and merge enough to reach masses millions or billions of times that of the sun.

Yet, since it began operations in 2022, the JWST has been routinely discovering supermassive black holes powering quasars as early as 400 million years after the Big Bang. If that wasn't confusing enough, the discovery of Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the third quasar pair seen at Cosmic Dawn, could really break current models.

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua was uncovered in data from the JWST's Aether survey, which is conducting a census of objects in the early universe. Using JWST’s NIRSpec (Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit) instrument, the survey has uncovered 200 quasars, just under half of all currently known early universe quasars. It was while browsing the Aether dataset that the team discovered that quasar J1602+4228A is not alone, it had a companion now designated J1602+4228B.

Resolving these two quasars should have been nearly impossible from the ground. But this was possible for Gemini North thanks to perfect timing and perfect weather conditions over Maunakea, the dormant volcano on the island of Hawai'i where the telescope is located.

A definite scientific feat, Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua remains a mystery for now, but it could actually help scientists better understand how galaxies were coming together during Cosmic Dawn, a vital stage in the evolution of the universe.

"Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," Onorato said. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times."

The team's results were published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

#867. How Pochettino came on Man Utd's radar - and what Carrick was told when

Pochettino was appointed USA manager in September 2024

Michael Carrick must have known what was coming.

Not just because reports of his imminent dismissal were widespread - followed by information about who would be replacing him as Manchester United boss.

But because, effectively, he and his representatives were given heavy enough indications of what was to follow.

On Monday, according to well-placed sources, Carrick's agent was contacted by chief executive Omar Berrada to be told he and director of football Jason Wilcox would be heading to Monaco for a planned meeting with co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe that would include a discussion about the head coach's future.

A day later, it is believed Wilcox had a similar conversation with Carrick.

It is understood that on both occasions it was communicated that a recommendation regarding Carrick's future at the club would be made.

What is not clear is whether Carrick and his representatives knew that recommendation was to relieve him of his duties.

By that point, BBC Sport has been told United were aware of a $10m (Â£7m) release clause in Mauricio Pochettino's contract with the United States national team. One source even indicated it was representatives of the Argentine who told the Premier League side.

There is some regret behind the scenes at United that machinations leading to Carrick's departure on Thursday were played out so publicly.

But with football clubs the size of United, keeping such developments completely private is extremely difficult - and there is a feeling they were as transparent with Carrick as they could be.

Following heavy defeats by Como and Bournemouth, United placed huge importance on the following three games - against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa.

It is understood United's leadership team were clear with Carrick that results and performances needed to improve. A defeat, a victory and draw weren't enough to save him.

There is a feeling that during that three-game period, there was not enough progress, particularly in terms of team structure - underlined by the fact they conceded eight goals.

Six PL games that defined Carrick's Man Utd tenure

Pochettino finalising Man Utd deal after Carrick sacking

The chaos that took Carrick from two-year deal to sacked within 15 games

Carrick has conducted himself with great dignity during the turmoil of the past few days and he leaves the club - certainly in the eyes of supporters - with his standing as a United great intact.

When United first appointed Carrick - initially on an interim basis following the sacking of Ruben Amorim in January - he had a positive impact on the squad, and subsequently results.

United liked his positive messaging to the players and media. They felt Carrick brought calm to rocky waters and protected his players at every opportunity - a contrast from at least the closing stages of Amorim's tenure.

On the pitch, the United hierarchy felt Carrick's style of play allowed the forward players more freedom, and they won 12 of their last 17 matches of the season.

While United considered other managerial options in the summer, there was ultimately a sense Carrick had earned a shot at the job on a permanent basis.

The 45-year-old signed a two-year deal, though it is understood United contractually protected themselves in the event of an early termination.

Part of the thought process was to provide the players with some managerial stability given the increased turnover of head coaches in recent years.

Yet the season started poorly with defeat at newly promoted Hull City - and has only spiralled downward since.

United are third bottom of the Premier League and 17th in the Champions League table.

What does Mauricio Pochettino need to succeed at Manchester United?

Since Monday, talks have been ongoing with Pochettino.

On Wednesday, Berrada contacted the US Soccer Federation to confirm the existence of the release clause and their intention to activate it.

It is understood the news did not come as a surprise to those across the Atlantic.

Pochettino had been clear with his employers about the discussions with United and - most pertinently - his intention to return to the Premier League.

While United want Pochettino in situ as soon as possible, they are respectful of the fact the USA have two fixtures against Haiti to play - the second of which is on 18 November.

If Pochettino takes charge of the second game, it is understood he will be in place at United's Carrington headquarters on 19 November - four days before they face Liverpool.

#865. Ultimate 1-50: the male footballers best associated with each squad number

Who is football’s most legendary No 9? Has there ever been a legendary No 28? And why exactly does Mario Balotelli love wearing No 45 so much? Here’s our list and the stories behind it

The relationship between players and numbers is a long-established one filled with memories and fascinating as well as fun stories behind them. With that in mind, the Guardian has had a go at deciding which male player is best associated with each squad number, from 1-50. Various factors were taken into consideration, including how long a player wore/has worn that number, what they achieved/have achieved in it, why they decided to wear it in the first place and, in some cases, how distinctly it has become associated with them in death. The below list is highly subjective and ultimately a bit of fun, but don’t let that stop you being shocked and furious in equal measure.

One is the loneliest number, but it also allows you to stand out – especially in football, where you play by different rules and wear different attire. Nobody stood out quite like Yashin, the almost mythical USSR and Dinamo Moscow goalkeeper of the 1950s and 1960s. He often wore a flat cap in goal, and his trademark kit led to the nicknames “Black Spider” or “Black Panther” (strictly speaking, it should have been the less catchy Very Very Dark Blue Spider). Yashin remains the only goalkeeper to have won the Ballon d’Or; with a respectful nod to Dino Zoff, Peter Schmeichel and others, he was a simple choice.

It would be a crime against dynamism and flair if we didn’t give one of the traditional full-back numbers to a Brazilian. Some of their great right-backs didn’t actually wear No 2 – Djalma Santos and Carlos Alberto, World Cup-winners of 1958 and 1970, sported No 4 – but that still leaves us with the richest pickings. It’s hard to look beyond Cafu, a bullet train on the right for Brazil, Roma, Milan and others. He won two World Cups and is the only man to play in three consecutive finals. Chuck in more than 700 club games, and that’s a mind-boggling amount of runs up that right flank.

Few could dispute this choice. Maldini is No 3. Milan retired his number – it can only be used again if one of his sons plays for the club – and it’s almost a surprise Fifa didn’t do the same. As a left-back or left-sided centre-back, Maldini came as close as anyone to perfecting defending; on the ultra-rare occasions he was given a chasing, by Chris Waddle or Karel Poborsky, it was a JFK moment. It’s an oddity that he didn’t wear No 3 at Italia 90 or USA 94. But for most of his career, to see Maldini with any other number would have been like seeing James Bond in a shell suit.

For longevity and sheer class – on and off the field – Zanetti pips Pep Guardiola, Sergio Ramos and the aforementioned Brazilian right-backs to this number. A Swiss Army knife of a footballer, Zanetti was one of the first players to show that the positions of right-back and centre-midfield spoke the same language. He won 16 trophies in 19 years at Inter, 15 of them as a quietly inspirational captain. José Mourinho said “it was an honour to coach him”, while Maldini called him “my most respected enemy”. As was the case with Maldini, Zanetti’s number was retired by a Milanese giant.

With apologies to Zinedine Zidane, Fabio Cannavaro and Obdulio Varela, the terrifying and granite-willed captain of Uruguay’s 1950 World Cup winners, this was never in doubt. Beckenbauer, libero and captain of the all-conquering West Germany and Bayern Munich sides of the 1970s, was born to stroll around a football field, No 5 on his back, an imaginary Andrex-soft sax jazz soundtrack playing in the background. His biographer, Uli Hesse, wrote that the number “became synonymous with his unique interpretation of the libero role”. Nobody did it better; nobody ever will, which is essentially why, quite rightly, Bayern retired their No 5 shirt in December 2024.

Iconography trumps tactics on this one. In modern football, a No 6 is a deep-lying midfielder, but in the 20th century it was indelibly associated with a specific genre of centre-back: captains, leaders, legends. The list is headed by Bobby Moore, Tony Adams and the don; Baresi, a manager on the field for Arrigo Sacchi and Fabio Capello during Milan’s golden age, his shirt retired by the club in 1997. Baresi died this year; if you have any doubts that he is the definitive No 6, just look at the pictures from his funeral in August of this year.

This probably should have been given to Garrincha, who wore No 7 when he single-footedly won the 1962 World Cup for Brazil, but you can’t argue with a trademark. Never mind the trifling matter of almost 1,000 career goals, CR7 is a brand that includes fragrances, underwear, footwear, lifestyle hotels, a fitness app … even bottled water. It all started in 2003, when Sir Alex Ferguson encouraged the teenager from Portugal to embrace one of the most iconic shirts in football – Manchester United No 7s include George Best, Bryan Robson, Eric Cantona and David Beckham. On a global scale, Ronaldo, now retired from international duty, is the most famous of the lot.

Desailly embraced the No 8 shirt when he was repurposed as a central midfielder at Milan then wore it when he played centre-half for the France team that won France 98 and Euro 2000. Desailly won the lot as a No 8, with the enduring memory of him in that number coming from the 1994 Champions League final, as the then 25-year-old rampaged through Barcelona to score the final goal. Xavi, for Spain, Andrés Iniesta, for Barcelona, and Socrates were strong shouts, all more traditional No 8s, but Desailly got the nod.

A choice that was painfully obvious, romantic and a bit dispiriting. Let’s start with the good stuff: Ronaldo 1.0 was the greatest young player we’ve ever seen, blessed like nobody before or since with the holy trinity of power, speed and skill. The dispiriting bit is that his Nike Mercurial R9 boots, unveiled in the buildup to France 98, catalysed an age of naked commercialism that football has never escaped. (Paradoxically, Ronaldo was wearing No 10 for Inter at the time, though that would soon change.) Let’s just remember the good stuff – R9, the first PlayStation footballer, and the platonic ideal of a distinctly Brazilian brilliance.

“No matter what happens and no matter who is in charge, the No 10 shirt will always be mine.” We’re not going to argue with Maradona, even if Lionel Messi, Pelé or Ferenc Puskas were the most compelling alternatives. To Maradona, the No 10 was a way of life, part of a uniquely Argentinian identity – that of the pibe, the creative genius from a poor background blessed with celestial skill and the vicious defiance of an alley cat. He even had the No 10 tattooed on his back. Close your eyes and you can probably see the font.

“I remember the first time I saw him,” said Sir Alex Ferguson. “He was 13 and just floated over the ground like a cocker spaniel chasing a piece of silver paper in the wind.” Giggs wore a lot of different numbers at the start of his career – 2, 4, 5, 7, 10 – but from the moment the Premier League introduced squad numbers in 1993, he was Manchester United’s No 11, even when he changed position in his dotage. There were other 24-carat contenders, including the Brazilian collective of Garrincha, Rivellino, Eder, Romario, Rivaldo and Ronaldinho, but none can match Giggs’s longevity or medal collection.

After an injury-ruined season with Milan, Van Basten started Euro 88 on the bench, both literally and numerically. He came in for the second game against England, scored a hat-trick and never looked back. A Hitchcockian late winner against the hosts, West Germany, was followed by an entirely preposterous volley in the final against USSR. From then on he was the Netherlands’ No 9. But the legend of No 12 endured, particularly when Thierry Henry was playing for France: he chose No 12 because of Van Basten. Were it not for the Dutchman, another Frenchman, the great Alain Giresse, would have been our choice.

The German sense of humour has always been underrated: they, more than any other country, have embraced the No 13 shirt. It’s been worn at major tournaments by Rudi Völler, Karl-Heinz Riedle, Michael Ballack, Thomas Müller – and Gerd Müller. He picked it for the 1970 and 1974 World Cups, and a triumphant Euro 72, as a nod to his childhood hero, Max Morlock, who scored in the 1954 World Cup final win over Hungary. Muller played 13 World Cup games and almost finished with 13 goals. The alternative ending was better: his 14th, in the 1974 final against the Netherlands, won the World Cup.

Cruyff’s first encounter with No 14 came by chance. Ajax’s Gerrie Muhren couldn’t find his usual No 7 shirt, so Cruyff gave him the No 9 and pulled the first spare shirt out of the bag. Ajax won, Cruyff kept wearing No 14 and embraced every connection: for example, he’d married his wife, Danny, on 2 December 1968 and pointed out that 2+12 and 6+8 both equal 14. The Cruyff Foundation later set up Schoolyard14, the key principle of which is the 14 Rules of Johan Cruyff. If he were a young footballer in 2026, Cruyff would be the first to have a symbol instead of a number.

This was the toughest of the teens, with nobody demanding selection. We plumped for a man who, as far as we can tell, spent only five games in the No 15 shirt. Falcão, an imperious box-to-box playmaker, missed all Brazil’s World Cup qualifiers for Spain 82 – Roma didn’t have to release him, so they didn’t – and as a result was not among Nos 1-11. But he played all five games at the tournament in the No 15 shirt and won the Silver Ball, which makes him officially the best player in the greatest attacking team many of us have ever seen.

Sham! Yes, it’s somewhat awkward having a certain era of Manchester City players on this list given “events” a few weeks ago, but, equally, it’s impossible to ignore them entirely given their achievements on the pitch, and that’s very much the case when it comes to Rodri, a man who completed football by the age of 30. He’s won the World Cup, the Euros, the Ballon d’Or, the Golden Ball, the Treble … the lot. When he moved to Barcelona in the summer, Rodri asked Fermin López if he could take the No 16 shirt that has served him so well. We assume it was a short conversation.

It’s all because of Wilfried Bony, you know. Bony was wearing No 14, the number Kevin De Bruyne wore at Wolfsburg, when De Bruyne moved to Manchester City in 2015. He picked No 17 instead. It’s apt there’s a “7” in there somewhere, such was De Bruyne’s devastating impact in the inside-right channel during his decade at the Etihad. His creative genius made him an irresistible choice, despite the appeal of Emmanuel Petit, Frank Rijkaard, Vitinha and even a young Cristiano Ronaldo. For a fair chunk of his time in England, De Bruyne was the best player in the best league in the world.

If you’re going to launch the toys, you might as well do it in style. When Ronaldo took the No 9 shirt at Inter in the summer of 1998 – the Brazilian had joined the club 12 months earlier and initially wore No 10 – the incumbent had an idea. Ivan Zamorano had worn No 9 for Chile, Sevilla, Real Madrid and Inter and took enormous pride in the symbolism of the shirt. So he switched to No 18 and had a plus sign stitched into the shirt: 1+8. Long before Lionel Messi, this was a different kind of false nine.

The Golden Ball winner at Italia 90 wore No 19. But enough about Toto Schillaci. Gascoigne’s unfettered, painfully innocent brilliance drove Bobby Robson’s team to the semi-finals of a tournament they were expected to stink out, and ultimately changed the game in his country. In 2009, England and West Germany met in a charity-match repeat of the 1990 semi-final. England wore Nos 1-11 – except Gascoigne, who had No 19 on his back. Robson, who died five days later, attended the match in a wheelchair. On the way home, he had one pressing question for his son: “How did Gascoigne play?”

Paolo Rossi, Clarence Seedorf and Ole Gunnar Solskjær are among those who have worn No 20 with great distinction but no one is, and probably ever will be, as synonymous with it as Jota. It was referenced in the song Liverpool fans sung about him with great lustre when he was alive and with great poignancy after he died, with the club’s retirement of the number and building of a ‘Forever 20’ memorial outside Anfield further tying the late Portuguese striker to the digits. Gone far too soon, Jota will never be forgotten.

The Italian was always a mature vintage, a smooth midfielder who could spot a pass from any angle. He could have played many of his games with a glass of wine in his hand and when he had his own vineyard, 21 Brut Rose was produced by Pratum Coller in honour of the great man’s squad number. No 21 adorned Pirlo’s back at Inter, Milan, Juventus and New York City, as he collected six Serie A titles and a couple of Champions League winner’s medals, not to mention a World Cup with Italy in 2006.

The 2007-08 Ballon d’Or was an inevitability for the magical Brazilian, who spent the year running riot with his third-choice of two little ducks. The attacking midfielder wanted No 8 or No 10 when he arrived in Milan but Gennaro Gattuso and Rui Costa were already in possession of those respective when he joined from São Paulo and the youngster was not going to mess with two legends. His time at Real Madrid, after a €67m move, was far less successful and Kaká returned to Milan after four years, taking back No 22 in the process.

With Raúl wearing No 7, Beckham needed a plan upon joining Real Madrid in July 2003. He turned to Michael Jordan for inspiration, asking for his iconic digits as he became a galáctico. When Beckham moved to LA Galaxy four years later, he stuck with No 23. “The connection with Jordan and how important the No 23 was, I just felt it was the right thing to do,” Beckham said. Sol Campbell was another strong contender for No 23 given he wore it at Tottenham and Arsenal, as was Marc-Vivien Foé, whose No 23 shirt was retired by Manchester City after his shock death in June 2003.

“I really hope to stay in the heart of this city so that one day, Napoli also retire the No 24,” Insigne said. The Naples-born forward spent 16 years with his boyhood club, which is certainly a good way to ingratiate himself with the fans, some of whom wanted him to take Maradona’s iconic No 10. “Maradona’s 10? I’m very superstitious, plus I wear 24 because it’s my wife’s birthday and it’s brought me luck,” Insigne said.

It says something about a player’s association with a number that his blessing is required before it can be passed on to someone else. And so it was in August 2023 that Zola gave Moisés Caicedo the go ahead to be Chelsea’s No 25, with no else deemed worthy of taking that status from the Italian for two whole decades. A bit much? Not really given the brilliance of Zola’s performances across seven seasons at the club. There was the skill, the goals, and that sense of joy that made him popular far beyond the boundaries of west London. Quite simply, everybody loved to watch Franco play.

Many academy graduates are desperate to rid themselves of their first squad number once they have settled into the first team but the Chelsea centre-back stuck with what he was given for 18 years. One of the reasons Terry did so was because he saw supporters getting it printed on their own shirts and did not want them to buy another. What a nice captain, leader, legend, and indeed why fix something that isn’t broke? When a mural of Terry and Antonio Conte was painted on to Stamford Bridge, the “26” was far more prominent than his face, which really does say something.

It was at Sampdoria where the No 27 became imprinted on Quagliarella’s back, and in tribute to his former teammate Niccolò Galli, who died in a road accident aged 17. “I have no doubt that had he lived, he would have been captain of Arsenal and of Italy,” Arsène Wenger said of Galli, who he managed in north London before his passing in February 2001. Quagliarella continued to honour Galli throughout his career, taking in moves to Udinese, Napoli and Juventus, every time ensuring he got the number he wanted. At Juve he spent two seasons with No 18, but the forward’s cherished number was with him for two Serie A titles.

History shows that No 28 is often discarded by those seeking fame and fortune – Cristiano Ronaldo had it at Sporting as a kid, Steven Gerrard likewise at Liverpool – but Touré wore it for four seasons at Arsenal, a period that saw him become an Invincible. That perhaps explains why, after a three-season dalliance with No 5, he reverted to what he knew upon joining Manchester City in July 2009, going on to win another Premier League title with this most random of numbers on his back. Quite clearly it meant a lot to him, and justifiably so.

“I have had it now for many years,” Havertz said of the number he’s worn at Bayer Leverkusen, Chelsea and Arsenal. “When I became a professional, I took it because it has some history with my brother – we used to take it always when we played video games together. Since then I just took it, and for me it’s the perfect number. I love to wear it in a red shirt again.” It’s as good a reason as any, to be honest, and given Havertz’s success in No 29, why he gets the nod over some other contenders, including Monaco-era Kylian Mbappé.

Sometimes it only takes a goal to etch a player into a club’s history, and when that goal is genuinely seismic, the number he wore at the time also takes on a grand status. And so it is that Grønkjær is our No 30 given that’s what the Danish winger had on when he scored Chelsea’s winner against Liverpool on the final day of the 2002-03 season. Chelsea subsequently secured Champions League football over Gérard Houllier’s side, which convinced Roman Abramovich to buy the club that summer and change Chelsea’s fortunes, as well as the landscape of modern football, for ever.

Upon signing for Manchester United in July 2015, Schweinsteiger was given the No 23 shirt. He quickly changed to No 31 and, really, that was no surprise given that was the number he wore throughout his golden 13-year spell at Bayern Munich, coming through the ranks to win eight Bundesliga titles and the Champions League. The midfielder kept it during his two years at United and also wore it during his two years at Chicago Fire. Quite simply Schweinsteiger is No 31 (albeit he mainly wore No 7 for Germany) and no one else comes close to challenging him on that.

This feels like a number that should have generated a lot of candidates but ultimately there weren’t many, and certainly no one as notable as Tevez. From the shock, awe and controversy of his three years at West Ham, to the rampaging success of his two-year spell at Manchester United, to the wild, wonderful and also controversial nature of his four years at Manchester City, Tevez well and truly made No 32 his own, going on to also wear it at Shanghai Shenhua and upon his return to Boca Juniors. With apologies to Joël Matip, but it wasn’t even close in the end.

This was an immediate lock-in given Cech’s reasons for taking this number upon joining Arsenal from Chelsea in 2015. He was 33 at the time, had played 333 games in the Premier League and – wait for it – 33 is number of vertebrae in the human spine. “Hope to be a part of the spine of the team,” Cech posted on social media on 11 July 2015. Seriously, what a guy. Speaking of Arsenal, Riccardo Calafiori was also in contention given he wore No 33 at Basel and Bologna before nabbing it upon his arrival at the Emirates two years ago.

The choice for this number came down to Nigel de Jong or Xhaka. The former wore it throughout his five seasons at Manchester City, four at Milan, one at LA Galaxy and one at Galatasaray. Strong but not strong enough given Xhaka wore it during his three seasons at Basel, four at Borussia Monchengladbach, five of his seven at Arsenal, two at Leverkusen and throughout his time so far at Sunderland. And here’s the clincher: the Switzerland captain adopted No 34 in the first place because that was the number of the bus he took to training when in the youth ranks at Basel. It just had to be him.

A couple of Argentinians were in the running for this number, namely Pablo Aimar, who wore No 35 at different times for Valencia and River Plate, and Diego Placente, who wore it throughout his five seasons at Bayer Leverkusen, a period in which he played an important role in them finishing runners-up in the Bundesliga and Champions League. But ultimately this was no contest given Akinfeev’s remarkable association with No 35, the Russian goalkeeper taking it on upon graduating from CSKA Moscow’s youth ranks to the first-team squad in 2003 and, 23 years later, still retaining it. That, folks, is dedication to your squad number.

Martín Zubimendi was a strong candidate for this number given the reason he adopted it upon joining Arsenal in July 2025 was because he also wore it when making his debut for Real Sociedad, his boyhood club, six years earlier. But, in the end, longevity overruled sentiment in favour of Darmian, who wore No 36 across a 10-year spell for Milan, Padova, Palermo, Torino, Manchester United, Parma and Inter. There doesn’t appear to be any specific reason why the Italian full-back was so wedded to such a random number, but he was, and for a long time.

Van de Ven has only worn No 37 for the past four seasons, ever since joining Tottenham from Wolfsburg in August 2023. He didn’t wear it while at the German club or at Volendam, where the Dutch centre-back began his career. But his reason for doing so is why he’s the clear choice. “A friend of mine passed away when we were young and it was always his favourite number,” Van de Ven revealed in a February 2024 interview. “So when I had the opportunity to choose No 37 when I signed for Tottenham … to be honest, it’s for him.”

Born in Australia and raised in Macau, Tombides joined West Ham’s academy in 2008 as a promising teenage striker. He had talent and dedication and made his first-team debut in a League Cup tie against Wigan in September 2012. That game came a year after Tombides had been diagnosed with testicular cancer. He died from the disease in April 2014, aged only 20. Shortly after, West Ham retired his No 38 shirt. It was only the second time the club had done such a thing, the first being with Bobby Moore’s No 6 shirt, a sign of just how well thought of young Tombides was in east London.

Guimarães chose No 39 upon making his debut for Athletico Paranaense in 2017 and has worn it ever since, at Lyon, Newcastle and now Arsenal, because it was the dispatch number of the taxi his father drove in Rio de Janeiro. Quite clearly it means a lot to the Brazil midfielder, as he explained in an article published by The Players’ Tribune in February 2023. “For me 39 is special. No, it’s more than that. It’s magical. It gave me everything in life”. Sorry Marcus Rashford in his first season at Manchester United, but you’re not topping that.

Idrizaj joined Swansea from German club Eilenburg in August 2009 as a promising 21-year-old striker. He went on to make three first-team appearances that season with plenty more seemingly on the horizon. But on 15 May 2010, Idrizaj died of a suspected heart attack while at home in his native Austria. It was a sad shock that led to Swansea retiring the former Liverpool player’s No 40 shirt. That showed how much everyone at the club thought of him, which was seen again when Swansea’s players wore T-shirts bearing Idrizaj’s name after winning the 2011 Championship playoff final.

Rice’s reason for wearing No 41 throughout his time in West Ham’s first team and ever since joining Arsenal in July 2023 is pretty straightforward. “It was a number I was given in the [West Ham] academy by the kitman, Jamo. It’s stayed with me since,” he said. “Regardless of what happens in my career, I might stay with 41. ‘Rice 41’ has a nice ring to it”. That’s debatable, but what’s for sure is that Rice has become distinctly associated with the number as he’s gone about establishing himself as one of the best midfielders in the world.

Touré chose No 42 upon joining Manchester City in July 2010 because it was the reverse of the No 24 he had worn at Barcelona. A simple if somewhat odd motivation that very much did not backfire as the Ivorian went about making the number his own during an eight-year spell at City that saw him win three Premier League titles, two FA Cups, two League Cups and become one of the most impactful, impressive midfielders on the planet. Touré retained No 42 upon joining Olympiakos in September 2018 before going back to 24 at his final club – Qingdao Huanghai in China.

“It was my first number in professional football, it’s a lucky number I guess”. Klich’s reason for wearing No 43 is, like with many others, based on what was given to him at the start of his career, which in Klich’s case occurred at Cracovia in his native Poland. He subsequently wore it for two seasons at PEC Zwolle, one at FC Twente, six at Leeds, two at DC United, one at Atlanta United and now back at Cracovia. Klich never wore No 43 at Wolfsburg, Kaiserslautern or Utrecht, so it clearly doesn’t mean that much to him, but he’s done enough to make it on this list.

Has a man ever loved No 4 as much as Perisic? It feels unlikely given he has worn various versions of it – namely “4”, “14” and “44” – throughout his career. He’s not No 4 on this list because that is Javier Zanetti, which is also the reason why Perisic couldn’t have No 4 upon joining Inter in August 2015 – the number had been retired by the club in honour of the Argentina great the previous year. Perisic subsequently took No 44, which the Croatian also wore at Club Brugge and Borussia Dortmund. That’ll do as far as this list is concerned, especially given his only real rival is Massimo Oddo.

Why [always] him? Well, it could’ve been Roméo Lavia or one or two others, but ultimately it had to be the man who wore No 45 with great fuss and furore at Inter, Manchester City and Liverpool before also doing so at Milan, Brescia, Monza, Adana Demirspor, FC Sion and Genoa. No 45 has become the number for one of the careers of the modern era and the association is only strengthened by its sweet origin story. As Balotelli explained: “When I first played with Inter, the numbers for young players were No 36 to No 50. I took No 45 because four plus five is nine – and I scored. It brings me luck.”

The Italian goalkeeper represented 12 different clubs in a 19-year career and only wore No 46 at one of them. But he gets the nod because of the nice, circular nature of the association. Sirigu wanted No 6 before making his Serie A debut for Palermo in 2009 but was told he couldn’t because it wasn’t appropriate for a keeper by the manager, and someone who knows a thing or two about shot-stopping, Walter Zenga. So he chose No 46 because it was the one worn by the legendary Italian motorcyclist Valentino Rossi. Sirigu left Palermo in 2011 before returning 13 years later. The number he chose upon doing so? 46.

This was a shoo-in for a couple of reasons: Foden has worn the number throughout his time as a first-team player at Manchester City, which is verging on a decade and seen him win everything going, and because of the origin story. Foden’s grandfather Ronnie, a big City fan, passed away when he was only 47. “I was young when we lost him,” said Foden in a 2024 interview. “My dad said he loved playing football with me and that it would be amazing if I took the shirt number. I have loved it ever since.” Foden’s tribute to Ronnie extends to having “47” tattooed behind his right ear.

There’s no point sugarcoating it – this is a stretch. Jones only wore No 48 for two years at Liverpool, from 2018-2020, and there appears no interesting reason for him doing so. But the midfielder gets the nod because the competition is razor-thin bordering on nonexistent. It certainly helps Jones’s cause that he wore No 48 when scoring the winner in Liverpool’s FA Cup third-round victory over Everton at Anfield in January 2020. It was a superb, long-range curling finish that made Jones, at 18 years and 340 days, Liverpool’s youngest goalscorer in a Merseyside derby since Robbie Fowler in March 1994.

“Forty-nine, forty-nine, Lewis-Skelly” sing Arsenal supporters in praise of their academy graduate as well as in recognition of why he has kept hold of such a random number even after establishing himself in Mikel Arteta’s first-team squad. Lewis-Skelly was given the choice of changing to a more established number ahead of last season but stuck with No 49 because of its association with Arsenal’s Invincibles-era unbeaten run of games, and an Arsenal song ever since (‘Forty-nine, forty-nine undefeated’). Sound reasoning and enough to earn the 20-year-old a place on this list ahead of Ronaldinho, who wore No 49 at Atlético Mineiro and Querétaro.

Another shoo-in given the unsurprisingly sparse options for this number and the fact Markovic has worn it for the bulk of his long, nomadic career. He first adopted it when he broke through at Partizan Belgrade in 2011 and continued to do so at Benfica and Liverpool, as well as at Fenerbahce, Hull and Anderlecht – who he joined on loan during his time at Anfield – before taking it again upon his permanent return to Partizan in 2019. The Serbian winger has since gone on to wear it at Gaziantep FK, Trabzonspor, FC Baniyas and Apollon Limassol. Markovic is No 8 at current club, FK Cukaricki, but clearly, at heart, he’s Mr No 50.

Who have we missed from our this ultimate 1-50 list? Tell us the male player (or players) we should have included and why. Feel free to let us know why they mean so much to your club or country. Let us know in the form below.

#864. 'A lie' & 'nonsense' - Palmer committed to England, says Rogers

Cole Palmer and Morgan are Chelsea team-mates

Morgan Rogers says any suggestion Cole Palmer is not committed to England "is a lie" and "nonsense".

Rogers scored the opener in Wednesday's 2-1 Uefa Nations League win over Croatia, with Harry Kane adding a penalty on his record-breaking 126th appearance for the men's side.

But his Chelsea team-mate, and childhood friend, Palmer had been left out of the squad after boss Thomas Tuchel said he "misses too many chances to impress".

The 24-year-old Palmer, who was also not called up for the World Cup, withdrew from the previous England camp in September citing a minor injury.

Forward Rogers, also 24, was asked about the criticism of Palmer following the win at Wembley, and told BBC Radio 5 Live: "He wants to be here.

"He wanted to get called up and he wanted to come and represent his country as he always has done.

"He was in quite a low place with his injuries last year and didn't feel 100% himself on the pitch, so he wants to be here and he wants to be the best version of himself.

"But he also has to look at his body. He wants to play for 10 or 15 years, he also has to manage himself. If he has to manage himself in the short term for the greater good then he has to do that and you have to fully support it.

"It has nothing to do with England or not wanting to play with England. It's a nonsense really that people are questioning someone that wants to play for England. It's a lie.

"You see the joy and smile on his face, how much he loves the game, so I honestly don't get it and he doesn't get it."

Is Palmer's England career over under Tuchel?

A must pick or unreliable? Tuchel's Palmer dilemma

History for Kane but what would England do without him?

In the three years since his England debut, Palmer has only won 14 caps, scoring two goals - including one in the Euro 2024 final defeat by Spain - and having one assist.

That is despite scoring 50 Premier League goals with 24 assists.

He was named England's men's player of the year for the 2023-24 season after some impressive form, including his strike against Spain in the Berlin showpiece.

But Palmer has only featured in three of Tuchel's 27 games since he succeeded Gareth Southgate as manager.

Some sketchy form last season, though, meant the former Manchester City player missed out on the the summer World Cup, with England going on to finish third after losing to Argentina in the semi-final.

He was named in Tuchel's first squad after that, but withdrew despite having played in all Chelsea's league games to that point.

Tuchel said this week: "We have enough number 10s and we stick to the guys who were in the previous camp because we were happy with the two and a half weeks we had together.

"I guess everyone is desperate to play for England and Cole is no exception.

"We are speaking now about a player that is not in camp. It counts when you are in camp and I just said last time that he misses too many opportunities to impress."

But the German added: "It's not personal. We will never assume Cole is in the mindset never to come to the camp.

"Cole is always in our mindset but the competition is on."

Record-breaker Kane scores winner as England qualify for quarters

Kane's top 10 England moments - which was your favourite?

Palmer should not give up hope of getting back into Tuchel's good books.

Last October, Jude Bellingham was left out of the squad for a friendly against Wales and a World Cup qualifier against Latvia.

The Real Madrid midfielder then ended up being a key part of the England team at the World Cup, scoring seven goals.

Former Three Lions goalkeeper Paul Robinson added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "You can see what Tuchel is doing when you look at what he's done with Jude Bellingham.

"It was only 12 months or so that Bellingham was getting left out of an England squad. Call it what you want, but it was management from Tuchel to make Bellingham realise that he wasn't the lone star of this team - the team was the star.

"The team was better with Bellingham in it, playing at his highest level.

"There was a lesson in his management skills with Bellingham and I wouldn't be surprised if he's doing the same now."
